t.koh ker archaeological site of ancient l:
For a few short decades in the tenth century, the capital of the Khmer empire was not at Angkor but here, deep in the forest of northern Cambodia. King Jayavarman IV established his court at Koh Ker, then called Lingapura, and in less than twenty years his builders raised dozens of temples across a wide area, before the capital returned to Angkor. The jungle took the city back. Today Koh Ker is a scatter of brick and sandstone sanctuaries among the trees, and in 2023 it was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list.

The centrepiece is Prasat Thom, a seven-tiered stepped pyramid that rises steeply above the surrounding forest. It looks more like a Mesoamerican temple than anything at Angkor, and it is an astonishing sight when you emerge from the trees. Around it lie dozens of smaller temples, some with enormous lingas, others with doorways framed by carved sandstone, many half-collapsed and overgrown with roots and moss. Compared with Angkor, the crowds here are tiny, and you can often wander alone among the ruins, listening to birds and insects.

Cambodia's recent history is never far away. The area was heavily mined during the decades of conflict, and although clearance teams have made the main sites safe, it is essential to stay on marked paths and not to wander into the forest. Local guides know the ground and are worth hiring.

The ride from Siem Reap takes a couple of hours or more, passing the huge, ruined temple of Beng Mealea, which is worth a stop in its own right: a sprawling complex swallowed by the forest, with walkways over the collapsed stones. The roads are now paved for most of the way, with long straights through rice paddies and villages, but watch for potholes, cattle, dogs, scooters and trucks. Further north, the road continues towards Preah Vihear, a temple perched on a cliff at the Thai border, with an extraordinary view over the plain.

Fuel is sold in villages along the way, sometimes from glass bottles at roadside stalls, but fill up in Siem Reap or larger towns when you can. Bring water, a hat and sun protection; the heat can be intense, especially from March to May. The rainy season, from June to October, makes the forest lush but can turn dirt tracks to mud. Cambodia drives on the right.
t.banteay srei@13.6,104.0:
Most people come to Angkor for the giants, Angkor Wat and the Bayon, but the temple that many remember best is small, pink and astonishingly intricate. Banteay Srei, the "citadel of the women", stands about twenty-five kilometres northeast of the main Angkor group, and it was consecrated in 967, earlier than the great royal temples. It was built not by a king but by a high-ranking courtier, the Brahmin Yajnavaraha, and dedicated to Shiva. Its reddish sandstone is fine-grained and easy to carve, and the result is decoration so delicate it looks almost like woodwork: lintels with scenes from Hindu epics, female guardian deities in niches, and foliage spiralling across every surface.

The temple is surrounded by moats and enclosures, and its scale is intimate, with doorways so low you have to stoop. French archaeologists restored it in the 1930s using a technique called anastylosis, rebuilding with original stones, and it became the first temple at Angkor to be restored this way. The temple was also the scene of a famous theft in 1923, when the young French writer André Malraux tried to remove carved figures and was arrested, an episode that later fed into his novel.

The ride from Siem Reap is a pleasure, at least once you leave the town traffic behind. The road heads northeast through flat countryside of rice paddies, sugar palms and stilt houses, with villages selling palm sugar along the roadside. The surface is generally good, the gradients nil, and the main hazards are cows, dogs, scooters and children on bicycles. Beyond Banteay Srei, the road continues toward the Phnom Kulen hills and the riverbed carvings of Kbal Spean. The dry season, from November to March, is the best time to visit; the rainy season brings humidity and downpours, and the hot season is fierce.

Fuel is easily found in Siem Reap, and roadside stalls in the villages sell petrol in bottles. There are food stalls and restaurants near the temple entrance, serving Khmer dishes such as amok, a fish curry steamed in banana leaves, and fresh coconuts. You will need an Angkor pass to enter. Arrive early, when the light makes the pink stone glow and the crowds are thin, and take your time with the carvings. The detail repays patience.
t.dong phayayen khao yai forest complex@14:
Thailand's first national park lies just a couple of hours from Bangkok, and it still has wild elephants walking down its roads. Khao Yai, established in 1962, covers a large area of forested hills on the southern edge of the Khorat plateau, and together with neighbouring protected areas, it forms the Dong Phayayen-Khao Yai Forest Complex, listed by UNESCO in 2005. The forests here are a mix of evergreen and deciduous, grasslands and streams, home to elephants, gibbons, hornbills, deer, and a small number of tigers.

The main road through the park climbs from the southern entrance near Pak Chong up into the hills, with tight, steep curves, good surfaces and lush forest on both sides. At the top, side roads lead to waterfalls, viewpoints and visitor centres. Haew Suwat waterfall is famous for its appearance in the film The Beach, and Haew Narok, a series of high falls, is impressive in the rainy season. Watch out for macaques by the roadside, which can be aggressive, and for elephants on the road, especially in the evenings. If you meet one, stop, keep your distance and give it time; never try to pass close.

The roads are open to motorcycles, though there is an entrance fee and sometimes restrictions on hours, particularly at night. Speeds are strictly limited to protect wildlife. The best time to visit is during the cool season, from November to February, when the air is fresh and the skies are clear; in the rainy season, from May to October, the forest is lush and the waterfalls are at their best, but the roads can be slippery and leeches lie in wait for anyone walking in the forest.

Outside the park, the area around Pak Chong has become a popular weekend escape for Bangkok residents, with resorts, cafés, farms and vineyards in the cool hills, which produce some of Thailand's best-known wines. On weekends and holidays, traffic can be heavy. The road along the northern edge of the park and the quieter routes toward Wang Nam Khiao offer good riding through farmland and forest.

Pak Chong has fuel, shops and restaurants of every kind, and Khon Buri, around thirty kilometres away, is a smaller town to the north-east. Try som tam, the spicy papaya salad of the north-east, with grilled chicken and sticky rice, and finish with a glass of fresh milk from the dairy farms of the area, a local specialty.
t.san cristobal de la laguna@28.5,-16.3:
La Laguna was the first Spanish colonial town not built behind walls, and its plan, a grid of straight streets around open squares, became a model for towns in the Americas. It was founded in the late fifteenth century, after the Spanish conquest of Tenerife, and for centuries it was the island's capital, with a cathedral, convents, a university from the eighteenth century, and tall houses with carved wooden balconies. UNESCO listed the old town in 1999. The city is cool and often misty, because it sits at about five hundred metres on a plateau where the trade-wind clouds gather, and the fine drizzle that drifts in from the north-east is a local fixture.

On foot, the old town is a joy. The streets are quiet in the morning, and the squares are lined with arcades and balconies of dark pine. The cathedral, the church of the Conception with its tall tower, and the main street of shops all merit a wander, and the students from the university give the evening cafes life. Local food includes papas arrugadas, the small wrinkled potatoes boiled in salty water, served with a spicy red mojo sauce, and there is excellent local cheese.

The riding from here is superb. To the north-east, the Anaga mountains rise in a knot of sharp ridges and laurel forest, with a road that climbs through tight bends and dense cloud forest to viewpoints over the sea. The surface is mostly good, but mist, rain and wet leaves make it slippery, so go with care. In the other direction, the long climb to Teide National Park on the high road gives you an entire change of landscape, from forest to black lava and pale pumice, with the volcano reaching 3,718 metres.

Fuel and workshops are plentiful, since La Laguna is a city of around a hundred and fifty thousand and runs straight into Santa Cruz. Parking in the old town is awkward, so use a garage on the edge. The weather changes quickly, so carry a rain jacket even when the south is baking. The light after a morning shower, soft and silver over the old roofs, is the best time to look.
t.khao yai national park@14.4,101.4:
Khao Yai was the first national park in Thailand, set up in 1962, and today it forms the heart of a vast forest complex, Dong Phayayen-Khao Yai, that UNESCO listed in 2005. It stretches across mountain ridges, evergreen forest, grassland and the sources of several rivers, and it protects some of the richest wildlife in mainland Southeast Asia: wild elephants, gibbons whose calls ring across the valleys at dawn, hornbills with their huge casques, macaques, sambar deer and, in the thick of the forest, a few tigers and bears that almost nobody sees.

The park road, Route 2090, climbs from the plateau town of Pak Chong, crosses the high ground and descends the other side toward Nakhon Nayok, a ride of about forty kilometres with a continuous series of bends, hairpins and gradients through tall forest. The tarmac is good, but the surface can be wet, and the real issues are wildlife and visitors. Elephants wander across the road, particularly at dusk, and when they do you must stop at a distance, switch off, and wait, because a wild elephant can easily be dangerous. Monkeys will steal from a parked bike. Speed limits are low and enforced, and there is an entrance fee for the park, with a fee for vehicles.

The higher parts of the park stand at roughly a thousand metres, much cooler than the plains, with mist in the mornings and a surprising chill after rain. Two waterfalls are the best known, Haew Suwat, which featured in a film, and Haew Narok, which drops in three stages. Both are reached on short walks. In the dry season, from November to February, the air is clear and the nights are cool, while from May to October the rain is heavy and leeches appear on trails.

Nakhon Nayok, the nearest big town, has fuel, restaurants and shops, and Pak Chong on the other side has a larger choice, along with the roadside restaurants known for steaks and the vineyards of the area.

Early morning is the best time to ride and to watch wildlife, with mist on the grass and gibbons calling. Bring a rain jacket, insect repellent and a lot of patience for animals on the road.
t.las palmas@28.1,-15.4:
Las Palmas is a city that does not look like most people's idea of a Spanish island. It is large, with nearly four hundred thousand people, it sprawls along a narrow neck of land between two seas, and it is the busiest port in the Canary Islands. The beach of Las Canteras, a long curve of sand sheltered by a reef, runs right through the city, and the old district of Vegueta, with its colonial plazas and the cathedral, recalls the days when ships bound for the Americas stopped here for water.

Columbus is said to have stopped on Gran Canaria on his first voyage in 1492, and the Casa de Colón, a museum in a beautiful old mansion, tells that story. The island is also known for its climate. Although only a day's sail from Africa, Gran Canaria enjoys mild temperatures all year thanks to the trade winds, which is why it is nicknamed the continent in miniature. Within a short ride you pass from dry southern desert to green northern forest.

That is what makes the mountain loop so good. From the city, roads climb through Arucas, with its banana plantations and a large neo-Gothic church made from dark volcanic stone, then up into the central highlands. Here the landscape turns dramatic: deep barrancos, pine forest, and the rock tower of Roque Nublo, a symbol of the island. The road to Pico de las Nieves, the island's highest point at nearly 1,950 metres, offers wide views, sometimes above a sea of cloud. Roads are narrow and twisty, with sheer drops, and the surface is usually good. Mornings can be cloudy on the north side, and the south is sunnier.

Fuel is no issue in the city or the larger towns, but up in the mountains there are few stations, so fill the tank beforehand. Take a jacket, because temperatures drop quickly with altitude. Stop at a village like Tejeda for almond sweets and coffee, and try papas arrugadas, wrinkled potatoes with spicy mojo sauce.
t.ta phraya national park@14.2,102.9:
Ta Phraya is a protected forest on the Thai side of the Cambodian border, and it forms part of one of the great wildlife refuges of Southeast Asia, the Dong Phayayen–Khao Yai Forest Complex, which UNESCO listed in 2005. The complex stretches over hills and plains in several provinces, and it holds one of the largest remaining populations of Asian elephants in the country, as well as gaur, sambar, tigers in small numbers, gibbons and four species of hornbill. At dusk the great hornbills fly across the clearings with a rushing, wing-beating sound that carries a long way.

The forest changes with the altitude. At the lower edges, dry dipterocarp woods with grass and bamboo give way to evergreen forest in the hills, and streams run clear over rock in the rainy season. The park lies in Sa Kaeo province, in a landscape of low hills, farms and plantations, and the border with Cambodia is not far. For that reason, military and border police are present in the area, and checkpoints are common. Carry your passport and bike papers, be polite, and avoid photographing military sites.

Roads leading to the park are generally paved and quiet, with gentle bends through farmland and rubber plantations, sugarcane fields and small villages. Signs are mostly in Thai, so use a map, and be careful of ox carts, motorbikes without lights and dogs. Inside the park, tracks may be unpaved and seasonally closed, and you should check with the park office whether a route is open. In the rainy season from June to October, heavy showers turn dirt to mud and leeches appear in the forest. The cool, dry months from November to February are the most comfortable time for riding and wildlife watching.

Fuel is available in towns on the plain, and the nearest big ones lie some distance away, so fill the tank before you head to the park. Roadside stalls sell grilled chicken, sticky rice, som tam papaya salad and cold drinks, and a local noodle shop will do a bowl of soup for very little.

Wild elephants are a real hazard on forest roads at dawn and dusk, so keep your speed low and your distance generous.
t.tombstone territorial park@64.5,-138.2:
Where the Dempster Highway climbs out of the boreal forest and breaks through the Ogilvie Mountains, the landscape changes in a rush. Tombstone Territorial Park lies about seventy kilometres above Dawson City's turn-off and protects a wilderness of jagged granite peaks, glacial valleys and open tundra, with Tombstone Mountain itself standing like a dark fang above the rest. The country belongs to the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in First Nation, who have hunted and travelled here for thousands of years, and the park was created with their involvement.

The Dempster is not an easy road, and its reputation is deserved. It runs some seven hundred kilometres from near Dawson City to Inuvik on the Arctic coast, mostly gravel, crossing two mountain ranges and the Arctic Circle. It was opened in 1979 and named after Inspector W.J.D. Dempster of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who in 1911 led the search for the lost patrol that perished while trying to reach Dawson by dog sled. Sharp rocks cut tyres, and rain turns the surface into slippery clay, so carry spare tubes, a repair kit and a plan. A tyre pressure that is low enough to give grip helps, as does a steady speed.

Within the park, the pass over North Fork Pass is the high point, with a visitor centre a little farther along that offers advice and information about conditions and walking trails. In late August and early September the tundra blazes red, orange and gold in colours that look painted, and it is the best time to be here, although the first snow can arrive in September. Summer brings long light, midnight sun farther north, and mosquitoes, and a headnet and strong repellent are worth carrying. Caribou, grizzly bears, and sometimes wolves roam the country, so keep distance and store food carefully.

Fuel is a serious issue. Camping at the park's campground is simple, with a pit toilet and water that needs treating. Turn around for a moment at the top of a pass, switch off the engine, and listen to the wind coming over the rocks.
t.chengdu@30.6,104.1:
Chengdu is the sort of city where the main achievement is that people there have a good time, and the rest is background. The capital of Sichuan province sits in a wide, humid plain in western China, home to more than seven million people in the city proper and a lot more in the wider area. It has an easy, teahouse-and-mahjong rhythm, a pace the rest of the country envies, and a cuisine whose reputation is global. Sichuan pepper, the tingling spice that numbs the lips, flavours the hotpot, the mapo tofu and the dan dan noodles, and a rider arriving here should plan on eating well.

The city is old. A famous irrigation system at Dujiangyan, built more than two thousand years ago, tamed the Min river and turned the Chengdu plain into one of the richest farming regions in China. Nearby, the bronze masks and gold work from the Sanxingdui site reveal a Bronze Age culture that left no written records. In the city itself, the Wuhou shrine honours the strategist Zhuge Liang of the Three Kingdoms period, and Du Fu, the Tang dynasty poet, lived in a thatched cottage that is now a park. The giant panda research base on the northern edge of the city is its most visited attraction, best seen early in the morning when the animals are feeding.

For riders, Chengdu is the start of the Sichuan–Tibet Highway, the southern branch of the G318 that crosses the Tibetan plateau toward Lhasa and is counted among the great overland journeys. From the plain the road heads west toward Ya'an and then climbs into mountains that shake off the humid haze, with high passes above four thousand metres farther along. Practical planning matters. Foreign travellers generally need permits, a local guide and temporary driving documents in China, and Tibet requires special permission, so the arrangements need to start well before arrival.

The city has everything a traveller needs, including fuel, spare parts and large shops. Traffic is heavy and city air can be hazy, so leave early. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for the road west, while summer rains bring landslides, and winter closes some high sections with snow.
t.akureyri@65.7,-18.1:
Akureyri calls itself the capital of the north, and with a bit under eighteen thousand people it is the second city of Iceland by some margin. It lies at the head of Eyjafjörður, the longest fjord in the country, with steep snow-streaked mountains rising straight from the water on both sides. The air is sharper than in Reykjavik and the winters are colder and drier, and in summer the town has a gentler, greener feel than most of the island. The church, a tall concrete building designed by the architect Guðjón Samúelsson and completed in 1940, stands above the town at the top of a flight of steps, and its stained glass includes a window rescued from a church in Coventry after the war.

The town is full of small pleasures. The botanical garden, one of the northernmost in the world, grows a surprising range of plants, and a good deal of the town's life revolves around a geothermal swimming pool with water slides and hot tubs. Traffic lights in the centre are shaped like red hearts, a local touch. Ice cream is taken seriously here, even in winter. Whale-watching boats run from the harbour in summer, and the fjord is rich in fish.

For riders, Akureyri sits on the Ring Road, route 1, and offers a choice of ways out. East, the road crosses the Vaðlaheiði hill or passes through a toll tunnel, opened in 2018, toward the powerful Goðafoss waterfall and the volcanic landscape of Lake Mývatn. West and south, the road climbs over heaths and valleys toward Blönduós and the western fjords. The surface is generally good tarmac, with occasional gravel at roadworks, and the wind is the usual hazard, with strong gusts in valleys that can push a bike sideways. Check the forecast on the official road and weather sites, since conditions change quickly, and in winter many roads close.

Fuel, supermarkets and repair shops are all easy to find in town, and there are many cafés and restaurants serving lamb, fish soup and skyr. Prices are high, as everywhere in Iceland. The midnight sun in June and July means riding almost around the clock, and September can bring the first northern lights. Buy provisions here before heading to more remote parts.
t.husavik@66.0,-17.3:
Húsavík is the town that decided to make whales its trade and has done very well from the decision. It sits on the shore of Skjálfandi bay in north Iceland, facing across the water to the snowy peaks of the Tröllaskagi range, and a row of brightly painted wooden boats waits at the harbour for visitors. The bay is one of the best places in Europe to see humpback whales, along with minke whales, porpoises and sometimes blue whales, and tours run from spring to autumn, sailing out on old oak fishing boats. Many boats provide warm overalls, and you will be glad of them.

The town has a long past. According to the old sagas, a Swedish Viking named Garðar Svavarsson sailed around the island in the ninth century and wintered here, building a house, and the name Húsavík, bay of houses, is said to come from that. A white wooden church of 1907, with a red roof and an unusual cross-shaped plan, stands on the hill above the harbour, and the Whale Museum covers the animals' biology and the history of whaling. The town was thrown into the global limelight when a film about the Eurovision song contest used it as a setting, and locals enjoy the attention.

The riding to Húsavík from the west and south is pleasant, with the road running through open farmland and lava fields, with the great waterfalls of Dettifoss and Goðafoss nearby. The Arctic Coast Way follows the north coast, with views of the ocean and islands such as Grímsey beyond the Arctic Circle. Roads are generally paved but can be rough on side routes, and weather swings from calm and bright to cold and windy in minutes, especially in spring and autumn. In summer the midnight sun gives long evenings, and that is the best time for the whale boats, when the water is calmer.

Fuel is available in town, and the nearest larger centre, Akureyri, is about ninety minutes away. There are plenty of cafés and restaurants that serve fish and chips, lamb, and the famous Icelandic hot dogs. The geothermal baths on the hillside above the town offer a pleasant way to warm up after a cold day on the water. Book your whale trip a day ahead if possible, and dress warmly.
t.risco caido and the sacred mountains of:
Gran Canaria looks like a small island, but the interior is one of the most dramatic mountain landscapes in the Atlantic. The centre is a collapsed volcanic caldera, split by deep ravines, with crags like Roque Nublo and Roque Bentayga sticking out of it. For the island's pre-Hispanic people, who arrived about two thousand years ago, these rocks were sacred, and the whole area is now a World Heritage cultural landscape. Risco Caído is a cave complex where the early islanders carved out shrines and granaries, one of which seems to be aligned with the sun at the equinox, when a beam of light moves across the painted walls.

The village of Artenara, on the edge of the caldera, is among the highest on the island, with many houses cut into the volcanic tuff, cool in summer and warm in winter. Even the church is partly carved from the rock. The roads here are exceptional for riding, with long climbs, hairpins and shoulders of pine forest, and views that on a clear day reach across to Tenerife and the great cone of Teide.

Be prepared for changing conditions. The north side of the island is frequently covered in a layer of cloud, and the sea of cloud below the summit can look beautiful while making the road damp and cold. The south is dry and bright. In winter there can be frost at the top, and strong winds on the exposed ridges.

Artenara and Tejeda are small villages, with about fifteen hundred and twenty-three hundred people, so fuel is best taken in the larger towns closer to the coast. Tejeda is famous for almond sweets and cakes, and the almond blossom in late January and February turns the valleys pale pink. Plan for slow riding, plenty of photographs and a walk to one of the viewpoints at sunset.
t.ayutthaya river easy ride@13.8,100.1:
Nakhon Pathom lies only a short ride from this point, and it is arguably the oldest city in Thailand. It was a major centre of the Dvaravati culture, a Buddhist civilisation that flourished across the central plains from about the sixth to the eleventh century, long before the Thai kingdoms emerged, and the city's heart is the Phra Pathom Chedi, the tallest stupa in the world, at about 120 metres. A huge, bell-shaped monument covered in glazed orange tiles, it rises above the town like a golden mountain, and local people come to make offerings at its base, with the smell of incense and jasmine in the air. The present structure was built in the nineteenth century around an older, smaller shrine, at the command of King Mongkut and finished under his successors.

The city has about a hundred and eighteen thousand people, and the area around the chedi is lively with markets, food stalls and the daily bustle of a provincial capital. The region is known for pomelos, the giant, sweet citrus fruit, which are sold by the roadside from about August to October, and for good roast pork and noodle shops. In the city, the Sanam Chandra Palace, built by King Vajiravudh in the early twentieth century as a retreat, has a collection of European-style pavilions in a garden of ponds and lawns.

The riding in this part of the central plains is flat and easy, but traffic can be heavy. Nakhon Pathom sits on the busy main road between Bangkok and the west, and trucks, buses and scooters share narrow roads. Out in the countryside, lanes follow canals and irrigation channels through rice paddies and sugar cane, with the occasional water buffalo. The surface varies from smooth tarmac to potholed asphalt, particularly after rain, so keep your speed measured, especially at night when unlit vehicles can appear. The cool season, between November and February, is the best for riding, while April brings fierce heat and the monsoon begins in May.

Fuel, food and repair shops are plentiful in Nakhon Pathom, and it makes a sensible place to start or finish a ride from Bangkok, about an hour away. Early in the morning, monks walk the streets collecting alms, and the air is cooler, so it is a pleasant time to start. Try the local pork satay or a bowl of rice porridge. Bring a rain jacket, because showers can arrive quickly, even in the cool season.
t.mae hong son fly ride route photo pull o:
Khlong Luang is on the northern edge of the Bangkok sprawl, in Pathum Thani province, and it is a world away from the mountain roads of Mae Hong Son. The land here is flat delta, crossed by straight canals, and filled with suburban housing estates, factories, university campuses and the last few paddy fields. The name of the province means lotus city, and in the cool season the ponds are filled with pink and white lotus blossoms, which farmers grow for their flowers and seeds. Khlong Luang itself, a municipality of about a hundred and eighteen thousand, is home to Thammasat University's Rangsit campus and the large Wat Phra Dhammakaya, a vast temple complex with a golden dome.

The canals tell the story. The Rangsit canal system, dug in the 1890s under King Chulalongkorn, opened up the central plains to rice farming, and the straight waterways and old locks still carve through the landscape. The area was among the hardest hit by the great floods of 2011, which submerged much of the province for weeks, and many houses still have raised ground floors and flood marks.

Just north, Bang Pa-In, about ten kilometres from here, has a royal summer palace, a delightful mix of Thai, Chinese and European buildings set among lawns, ponds and clipped trees. It was used by the kings of Ayutthaya in the seventeenth century, abandoned after the city's fall, and rebuilt by Rama V in the nineteenth century. The Chinese-style pavilion, with its carved red and gold interior, is a particular highlight, and the gardens are a relaxing place to cool down.

Riding here is mostly practical. The area is a gateway out of Bangkok, and the roads are dominated by heavy traffic, with expressways, tolled sections and busy junctions, so the best strategy is to start early, ideally before dawn, to be well clear of the traffic by sunrise. The surface is generally good, but some surfaces are rutted by lorries, and rain brings oil and slippery patches. Expect heat and humidity for much of the year, and plan for a break in the shade.

Fuel stations are everywhere, as are convenience stores, noodle shops and coffee stands, so it is easy to top up and have a bite before the long ride north. Khlong Luang is also a good place to find a mechanic or tyre shop before heading out. The cool season, from November to February, is the most pleasant, and evenings by the canals are lovely, with the sound of frogs and the smell of cooking.
t.kluane lake@61.1,-138.4:
Kluane Lake is the biggest lake in the Yukon, a long cold sheet of water in the shadow of the Kluane Ranges, and its colour is a milky turquoise from glacial silt carried down by streams from the big ice fields to the west. It lies on the Alaska Highway, with the little settlements of Destruction Bay and Burwash Landing strung along its shore, and with the St Elias Mountains rising behind to heights that include Mount Logan, the highest peak in Canada at nearly six thousand metres, hidden behind other peaks and rarely visible from the road.

The name Destruction Bay comes from the storms that blow down the lake and wrecked the original road-building camp in the 1940s. The Alaska Highway was pushed through here in 1942 by the US Army in a matter of months, in response to the Japanese threat after Pearl Harbor, and the road has been rebuilt many times since, but permafrost still heaves and cracks the asphalt, and frost heaves and patches are marked with small flags. Ride with attention, as a bump in the surface can come on suddenly, and gravel patches are common where roadworks continue.

The lake is full of lake trout and grayling, and the country around is boreal forest and tundra, with Dall sheep on the hills above the road, grizzly bears in the valleys, and moose in the willows. Bring bear spray if you intend to walk, and keep a sensible distance from any animal. Wind is the other thing: it funnels down the lake in the afternoon, and in autumn can be hard to ride in.

For fuel, the settlements of Destruction Bay and Burwash Landing have small stations and cafés, but their hours can be short and stocks limited, and the next larger places are Haines Junction to the east and Beaver Creek to the north-west, so it pays to fill up when you can. Summer brings nearly endless daylight, and the long evenings invite a late stop on the shore. Mosquitoes, especially in June and July, are fierce.
t.whitehorse@60.7,-135.1:
Whitehorse sits on the Yukon River in a broad valley under bare hills, and with some twenty-three thousand people it holds around three quarters of the territory's population, which gives you a sense of how empty the rest of it is. It is also where everything you need is available, fuel, repairs, food and beds, before the long road west. The Alaska Highway runs straight through town, and the town sits at about Mile 918 of that famous road, counted from Dawson Creek in British Columbia.

The name comes from the White Horse Rapids that once ran through Miles Canyon, just upriver of town, where the foaming water reminded gold-rushers of a horse's mane. In 1898, thousands of prospectors heading for the Klondike built boats at Bennett Lake and ran those rapids, and many were wrecked, until a tramway and then a dam tamed the river. A few minutes from the centre you can walk across a suspension bridge above the green canyon. The big sternwheeler SS Klondike, which carried goods down river to Dawson, sits restored beside the water, and the town's fish ladder, among the longest wooden ones in the world, lets Chinook salmon climb past the dam in July and August.

For the Kluane Scenic Drive, Whitehorse is the start: about 160 kilometres of Alaska Highway west to Haines Junction, where the St Elias Mountains and the Kluane ice fields rise. The road is mostly open, rolling and well surfaced, but frost heaves, patched asphalt and roadworks appear every summer, and it is a long, steady ride more than a technical one. Wildlife includes moose and the occasional bear near the highway.

Summer light is the unique thing: in June the sun barely sets, so a late departure is perfectly practical. Weather can still turn cold and wet at any time, and in winter this is a place of deep cold and aurora, not riding. Fill the tank, buy water and snacks, and expect long gaps between services.
t.litang@30.0,100.3:
Litang is one of the highest towns in the world, at roughly four thousand metres, a Tibetan settlement on a wide grassy plateau in western Sichuan, where the G318 highway crosses on its long journey from Chengdu to Lhasa. The mountains around it are rounded and bare, the sky is huge and the air is thin enough that every staircase becomes a conversation with your lungs. The pin sits right on the town, so fuel, food and basic lodging are close.

The G318, known as the Sichuan-Tibet Highway, is one of the great road journeys of Asia, and this section is among its most beautiful. The road climbs over passes above four thousand metres, crosses wide grasslands dotted with yaks, and drops into canyons with prayer flags on every bridge. The surface is usually good, though landslides and roadworks can interrupt it, and altitude sickness is a real risk. Acclimatise slowly, and do not rush the stages. Winter is cold and snowy, summer is bright and often wet in the afternoons.

Litang is famous for its monastery, a big Gelug complex founded in the late sixteenth century under the Third Dalai Lama, and for its annual horse festival in August, when riders from across the plateau gather to race and show their skill. The Seventh Dalai Lama was born near here, and Litang's long history has made it a spiritual centre for the region. Tibetan culture is strong here, with butter tea, tsampa and yak meat on the menu, and bright prayer flags fluttering from every roof.

A word of caution for foreign riders: China has strict rules about foreign drivers and motorcycles, and you cannot simply arrive and ride. A temporary licence, a registered vehicle and usually a guide are required, so plan well in advance and use a licensed operator. Roads, permits and checkpoints can change at short notice. If you are allowed to ride, wear warm layers and carry some altitude medicine, as the weather swings between sun and snow within the same hour.
t.sichuan giant panda sanctuaries wolong@3:
Wolong is a valley in the Qionglai mountains, about a hundred and thirty kilometres from Chengdu, and for many visitors it means one thing: pandas. The reserve, founded in 1963, covers a big stretch of forested mountain, rising from deep valleys to snow peaks of more than six thousand metres, and it holds one of the largest populations of wild giant pandas in the world. Together with other reserves in the region it was listed by UNESCO in 2006 as the Sichuan Giant Panda Sanctuaries, and the surrounding forest shelters red pandas, takins, golden monkeys and many rare birds.

The panda itself is a creature of narrow habits. It eats almost nothing but bamboo, up to a dozen kilos a day, and it lives in cool, damp forests between roughly 1,500 and 3,000 metres, where the bamboo grows thick under the trees. Wild pandas are shy and almost never seen, and a sighting is a matter of luck, but the research centre in the valley keeps captive pandas, and breeding programmes that have helped numbers recover. In 2008 the earthquake that struck Sichuan badly damaged the valley and destroyed much of the original centre, and the facilities have since been rebuilt.

The ride from Chengdu is itself a lesson in the geography of the region. The flat Sichuan basin, packed with fields, factories and villages, gives way quickly at the foot of the mountains, where the road follows the Min river past Dujiangyan, the ancient irrigation system built more than two thousand years ago, and then climbs through a deep, narrow valley. Tunnels, bridges and rock galleries mark the route, and signs of landslides and repair work are common. Rain and fog are frequent, particularly in summer, and the road can be closed by rockfalls with little warning.

Be realistic about services. Fill the tank in Dujiangyan or Chengdu before you start, because supplies in the valley are limited, and bring warm clothes since it is much cooler up the valley than in the basin. Visitors who want to ride in China should check the rules on licences and registration, which are strict and change. Spring and autumn are the best times, and mornings are the best hours, since the animals at the research centre are most active before the heat of the day. A bowl of Sichuan noodles and a pot of tea in a roadside restaurant completes the day.
t.ayutthaya river@13.9,100.7:
North of Bangkok the land is so flat that canals are the only landmarks. The pin falls in Pathum Thani province, around Khlong Luang and the Rangsit district, a quarter of an hour's drive past the airport at Don Mueang, where the city's suburbs thin into rice fields, warehouses and housing estates. The label points to Ayutthaya, the old capital, about fifty kilometres further north, and this is the sort of place a ride back from there ends up.

The canals are the reason for the town's shape. In the 1890s a company led by a prince dug the Rangsit Canal and a grid of side channels across the plain to open it up for rice farming, and the area took its name from Prince Rangsit. The long straight waterways still cut across the landscape, lined with houses and temples, and the fields between them turn bright green after the rains. Many of the old rice fields are now gone under factories and universities, and Thammasat's Rangsit campus occupies a large piece of land at Khlong Luang.

Ayutthaya itself was the capital of Siam for four centuries until the Burmese army sacked it in 1767, and its ruined temples and brick towers, scattered along the Chao Phraya River, are a World Heritage site. Riders returning from there follow the highway or smaller roads beside the river, past boat landings, small shrines and sugar-palm trees. Surfaces are generally good, but traffic is heavy, with lorries, vans and motorbikes crowding the lanes, and the rainy season, from May to October, brings sudden storms. November to February is cooler and more pleasant.

Fuel and food are easy everywhere. Stations line the main roads, and night markets set up in the evening with grilled meat, noodle soups and fresh fruit. Khlong Luang has shops and a big market, and Ban Lam Luk Ka offers more. Watch for motorbikes crossing lanes and for water on the road after rain.
t.mae hong@13.6,100.3:
The sea smells different at Samut Sakhon. The coordinates fall on the low coastal plain west of Bangkok, near the city of Samut Sakhon, whose old name, Mahachai, is still used for its fishing port and market. The Tha Chin River winds through town to the Gulf of Thailand, and the land around is a flat patchwork of fish ponds, mangroves and, near the shore, salt pans, where seawater is dried in shallow beds under the sun and raked into white heaps.

Samut Sakhon is one of the country's main fishing centres and processing hubs, and the harbour is thick with boats, nets and ice trucks. A huge seafood market starts before dawn, with baskets of shrimp, crab, squid and fish, and the town has a large community of workers from Myanmar, so the shops and food stalls offer Burmese tea leaf salad and curries as well as Thai dishes. A short train line runs from the market to the old railway at Mae Klong, and a small ferry crosses the river to temples on the other bank.

The ride from Mae Hong Son, the mountain province on the Burmese border, which this route nods to in its label, is a very long way north, so this finish is a gentle ending after the bends of the north. The roads here are flat and straight, with canals and ponds on both sides and long lines of lorries. Surfaces are generally decent, but busy and sometimes rough with patches of repair. Summer heat is heavy, and in the rainy season the roads can flood quickly. Early morning is the best time, when the air is cooler.

Fuel is easy, since stations are on every main road, and nearby Krathum Baen and Sam Phran have more services. For a meal, go to the market area for grilled seafood and crab curry, and be ready for fish sauce in everything. Watch for motorbikes and for slow trucks turning without warning.
t.siglufjordur@66.2,-18.9:
Siglufjordur is as far north as you can reasonably get on a paved road in Iceland, a small fishing town squeezed between steep mountains and a long narrow fjord on the Troll Peninsula. In the first half of the twentieth century it was the herring capital of the country, and during the summer the harbour was so crowded with boats and the town so full of seasonal workers that the population swelled well beyond what you see now. When the herring disappeared in the 1960s, the boom ended almost overnight. The Herring Era Museum, in a group of old waterfront buildings, tells the story well, with a salting station, workers' quarters and plenty of old photographs.

Today the town is quiet, with colourful wooden houses climbing up the slopes and a small harbour that often has a few fishing boats alongside. The mountains drop almost straight into the water on both sides, which gives the place a remarkable, enclosed feeling. In winter the snow can pile up, and in summer the midnight sun lights the peaks for what feels like days on end.

Getting here was once a serious challenge. For decades the only road came through the Strakagong tunnel, a narrow, unlit single-lane bore cut through the cliffs, and more recently the Hedinsfjordur tunnels have linked Siglufjordur to Olafsfjordur and Akureyri, shortening the journey and making the town far less isolated. The tunnels have a few single-lane sections with passing places, so ride cautiously, give way properly and keep your visor clear for the change from daylight to dark.

The road along the coast on the approach is some of the best riding in the north, with the water on one side, bare slopes on the other and a surface that is generally good. Wind can funnel hard along the fjords, so expect gusts, particularly on exposed corners.

With a population of just over a thousand, the town has a pump for fuel and a small supermarket, along with a couple of cafes and restaurants. Even so, I would arrive with a reasonable tank, because the next larger town, Dalvik, is a fair distance away. The hot pool is well worth an evening visit after a long day on the bike.
t.raufarhofn@66.5,-15.9:
Raufarhofn is a small fishing village on the north-east coast of Iceland, on the flat, empty Melrakkaslétta peninsula, a few kilometres south of the Arctic Circle. It was once one of the busiest herring ports in the country, and in the middle of the twentieth century the harbour was crowded with boats and the surrounding area full of salting stations. Today only a couple of hundred people live here, and many of the old buildings stand empty, which gives the place a faintly wistful atmosphere.

On the hill above the village stands the Arctic Henge, a modern stone monument that is still being built. It is intended to work as a sundial, aligned with the midnight sun and drawing on the old Norse mythology, and from the top you get wide views over the sea and across the lava and bog of the surrounding country. Not far to the north is Rifstangi, the northernmost point of the Icelandic mainland.

The landscape is very open, with low hills, shallow lakes, driftwood on the beaches and a huge sky. Birds nest here in huge numbers during the summer, including whooper swans, arctic terns and eiders, and the marshes are full of life. The light in the middle of the summer is long and golden, and the sun just dips below the horizon for a short time around midnight.

The riding is remote. Roads here are quiet and wide, and some sections are gravel, particularly on the minor routes, so check your route in advance. Wind is constant, and in winter snow and ice make the roads treacherous. Mobile signal can be patchy, and services are few and far between.

The village normally has a petrol pump and a shop, but opening hours are limited, and the next large towns are a long way away. Fill the tank earlier in the day, and bring food if you are planning to stay. It is a place for those who like remote country, silence and the feeling of having reached the edge.
t.tejeda@28.0,-15.6:
Tejeda sits in the crater-like bowl at the centre of Gran Canaria, with the great rock needle of Roque Nublo standing a short way to the south-west and the ancient shrine of Roque Bentayga showing on the skyline to the west. It is a white village of just over two thousand people, hung on a steep hillside at roughly a thousand metres, and it is regularly named among the loveliest in Spain for good reason.

The geology is the headline. Gran Canaria is a volcano whose old summit collapsed and eroded into a maze of deep ravines, and Tejeda lies in the middle of that landscape, with the island's high ground, including the Pico de las Nieves at nearly two thousand metres, rising around it. The sky is often brilliant, and the clouds drift in from the trade winds and get snagged on the rim, so it is common to ride out of a cold grey mist and arrive in full sun.

The roads here are the point. Tight, steep, switchbacked and often narrow, they climb to the Cruz de Tejeda viewpoint and wind down through the pine forest and the almond terraces, with big drops at the edge and views across the caldera that make you want to stop every few hundred metres. The surface is mostly good, but the corners are tight and blind, and the many tour buses and rental cars make passing a matter of patience. Be extra careful on wet mornings, when the moss and the mist can make the tar slick.

Tejeda is famous for almonds. In January and February the slopes flower white and pink, and the village sells almond sweets, marzipan and a dessert called bienmesabe, a thick almond cream that is exactly as sweet as it sounds. There are bars and small restaurants around the church square, and good coffee is never hard to find.

For fuel, do not count on a pump in the village itself; the nearest sizeable town is Vega de San Mateo, a little way east, and you should plan to fill up there before climbing. Artenara, higher up the road, is worth a detour for its cave houses carved into the volcanic rock, a way of living the islanders have used for centuries.
t.bangkok@13.8,100.5:
Bangkok is a city you meet with all your senses at once: the smell of charcoal grills and jasmine garlands, the sound of tuk-tuks and boat engines on the river, the heat that reaches you before you step out of the hotel lobby. About five million people live in the city proper and many more in the sprawl around it, and the Chao Phraya river is the thread that still holds the old centre together. The Grand Palace, Wat Pho with its huge reclining Buddha, and the temples of the old quarter sit along its eastern bank, and ferries cross the water for a few baht.

For a rider, Bangkok is the thing to leave early. Traffic is dense, the expressways have tolls, and the junctions are a thicket of motorbikes, so you will want to start at dawn, when the streets are quiet and the air is cooler. Follow the signs for Highway 1 north, or take the expressway and then peel off toward the old capital of Ayutthaya, about eighty kilometres away. Lane discipline is looser than in Europe, and overtaking happens on both sides, but traffic moves in a kind of rhythm you can learn to read.

Weather has a strong hand. The hot season peaks in April and May, with temperatures near forty, and the rains from June to October can drop a month's worth of water in an afternoon. November to February is cooler and drier and by far the best time to ride, though air pollution can be bad in the cool season. Always carry a rain jacket and drink plenty of water.

Bangkok has everything a motorcyclist might need: fuel on every major road, bike shops, 24-hour convenience stores and food at every hour. Start with breakfast at a street stall, perhaps a bowl of rice porridge with pork and a fried egg, and coffee with condensed milk. If you plan to ride a Thai-registered bike, keep your licence, passport copy and helmet with you, as police checks are common. Return in the evening and the river looks different, with the temples lit up and ferries gliding past.
t.historic city of ayutthaya@14.3,100.6:
For more than four hundred years Ayutthaya was one of the richest cities in Asia, founded in the mid-fourteenth century on an island where three rivers meet, and visited by Portuguese, Dutch, French, Japanese and Persian traders who all had their own quarters. Then in 1767 a Burmese army took it after a long siege and burned most of it to the ground. The Thai court moved south, eventually to Bangkok, and what remained became a field of brick ruins, the prangs and chedis standing above the grass. UNESCO listed the site in 1991.

You cannot see it all in one go, and the best way to travel between the ruins is to ride slowly around the island, or on a bicycle if you leave the motorbike parked. Wat Mahathat has the famous Buddha head caught in the roots of a banyan tree, a photograph everybody takes, and visitors are expected to crouch so that they do not stand higher than the head. Wat Chaiwatthanaram, on the riverbank, has a central prang surrounded by smaller ones, and at sunset the stone turns gold. Wat Phra Si Sanphet holds three bell-shaped chedis that once guarded the royal palace.

The ride up from Bangkok follows flat farmland and rice fields, and once you reach the town the roads are straight, slow and busy. Heat is the real challenge, especially from March to May, so do your sightseeing in the early morning and again late in the afternoon. Dress respectfully in temple areas, with covered shoulders and knees, and watch for stray dogs and tuk-tuks around the island, which slow without warning.

Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, the modern town, has more than eighty thousand people and no shortage of fuel, small restaurants and guesthouses. Boat noodles, a small and strongly flavoured bowl of beef or pork broth, are the local dish, and the riverside stalls are cheap. In November the cooler weather and the full moon festival make this a lovely time, with candles floating on the water, though the roads are busier and the temples more crowded.
t.pak chong@14.7,101.4:
Pak Chong sits on the road from Bangkok to the north-east, at the foot of the ridge that leads up to Khao Yai, and it is a town that makes a living serving two kinds of travellers: the weekend visitors who come to walk in the park and the long-haul drivers who push on to the plateau of Isan. The long strip of the Mittraphap Highway, Route 2, runs straight through the middle, with restaurants, farm shops and petrol stations. Locals call the surrounding country Thailand's wild west, because dairy cattle graze on the high green pastures and ranch-style steakhouses serve beef in a way that feels oddly Texan.

The real attraction is Khao Yai National Park, to the south, which was Thailand's first national park, set up in 1962, and now forms part of a UNESCO World Heritage forest complex. Tall evergreen forest, grasslands, waterfalls and wild elephants fill its mountains, and gibbons call at dawn. Wineries and vineyards on the slopes, a surprise to many, produce a pleasant if modest local wine, and cheese farms add to the sense of a rural holiday.

For riders, the road into the park climbs in a long series of bends through the forest, with the air getting cooler and the vegetation denser as you rise. The surface is generally good, but the road is narrow and winding, and drivers are sometimes impatient. In the park, animals cross the road, so keep your speed low, especially at dusk, and do not stop near elephants. The park authorities enforce rules, and entrance fees are charged. Weekends and holidays can be busy, so weekdays are quieter.

Pak Chong is a good-sized town with stations, cash machines and plenty of food, from roadside noodle stalls to restaurants selling steak. The local fuel stations are reliable, but the road into the park is long, so fill up in town. The best time to ride is from November to February, when the air is cool and dry, with views of mist over the forests. In the rainy season, from June to October, the forest is lush but leeches and heavy rain are likely.
t.khao yai park edge@14.4,101.4:
The edge of Khao Yai is a different country from the park itself. Where the forest road climbs from the plain, the hills above Wang Nam Khiao flatten into a high plateau of grass and farmland, with sunflower fields in the cool season, flower farms, and rows of fruit and vegetables, and the horizon is the dark wall of forest running up to the park boundary. The air here is cooler, and in the early mornings of December and January the valleys fill with mist that burns off by eight. It is easy to forget you are in the tropics.

The park sits on a high sandstone plateau, around eight hundred to a thousand metres, and its edge is steep, with the monsoon rain dropping on the windward slopes and feeding waterfalls on every side. Haew Suwat, a double cascade in the forest, appeared in a well-known film about backpackers, and is now a reliable stop for visitors. On the park's southern side, Haew Narok, a three-tier fall, is one of the largest in the country, and in the rainy season it thunders. Hornbills, gibbons and wild elephants live in the forest, and the elephants sometimes come out onto the roads.

Riding here is a matter of climbing and curving through the foothills. Roads from the Wang Nam Khiao side wind between farms and hills, with moderate gradients and good views, and the surface is generally decent, though tractors, trucks and cyclists use them. The route from Nakhon Nayok on the south side climbs through forest with long, tighter bends. Night riding is not wise, since animals cross the road after dark and drivers are sometimes erratic. Weekends are crowded with Bangkok visitors, so weekdays are calmer.

Small cafes and roadside stalls on the plateau sell coffee, grilled corn and fresh fruit. The best season is November to February, when the air is cool and the views clear. In the rainy season, expect fog, rain and leeches in the forest.
t.wang nam khiao hills@14.4,101.9:
Wang Nam Khiao is a highland district in Nakhon Ratchasima province, in the hills just south of the great forest of Khao Yai, and it is the kind of country Thai city dwellers go to when they want cooler air and green views. Its name means green water valley, and the valley is a patchwork of farms, resorts and orchards on a plateau a few hundred metres above the plains. The hills are the rim of a bigger system, the Dong Phayayen-Khao Yai Forest Complex, a UNESCO World Heritage site where wild elephants, gibbons, hornbills and tigers still live in the deep forest.

The area has changed rapidly in recent decades, from a quiet farming district to a weekend escape for Bangkok. Today, it is dotted with farm stays, cafes, small wineries and flower gardens, and the roads are lined with signs. Local farms grow cassava, corn, fruit and vegetables, and the cooler climate suits strawberries and grapes. The scenery is a series of rolling hills and open vistas, with the forest on the horizon.

The riding here is relaxed and enjoyable. Roads through the hills have gentle gradients and smooth bends, with fine surfaces in most places, though Thai roads are shared with trucks, pickups, motorbikes and the occasional dog, so keep an eye out. Drivers can be unpredictable, overtaking on blind bends or turning without warning, so give them space and ride defensively. In the rainy season, from May to October, afternoon downpours can flood roads and make surfaces slippery. The cool season, from November to February, is the best time, with clear skies and cool mornings, and sometimes mist in the valleys.

Nature is the draw. The forest teems with birds, and in the early morning, the air is filled with calls. Waterfalls flow in the wet season, and wildflowers bloom along the roads. Elephants occasionally cross the roads in the national park, so keep alert, particularly at dusk.

Services are scattered. There are PTT stations on the main roads and plenty of small shops, and the district has many cafes, with some serving good coffee grown in the region. Pak Chong, about forty kilometres away, is the main town for supplies, and has everything you need. Bring cash for small shops, and a rain jacket whatever the season.
t.pak chong food@14.7,101.4:
Pak Chong is the working town at the foot of the Khao Yai hills, strung along the Mittraphap Highway, the long road that runs from Bangkok across the plateau into the north-east of Thailand. It is a busy, unglamorous place with a lot of traffic and a lot of shopfronts, and it is the practical gateway to Khao Yai National Park, the oldest in the country. About fifty thousand people live in the area, and it feels larger because of the stream of visitors, truckers and weekend tourists passing through.

The town has an unusual identity. The cooler highlands around it have long been cattle and dairy country, and Pak Chong is known across Thailand for its steak restaurants and its roadside cowboy flavour, a curious blend of Isan and Texas. The dairy farms produce milk, yoghurt and cheese, and the fields around grow corn, grapes and sunflowers. The vineyards of the Khao Yai region, a recent development in Thai agriculture, produce wines that are a surprise to those who expect Thailand to be only tropical. Food in town ranges from noodle shops and night markets to grilled meats, and a bowl of noodles at a street stall is a good bet.

Riding in and out of Pak Chong takes some care. The highway is busy with lorries, buses and cars, and overtaking is common and risky. Traffic lights, roundabouts and u-turn lanes add to the confusion, so take your time. Once you leave the main road, the roads to the park and the hills become much quieter, with gentle climbs through forest and farmland. The road into Khao Yai itself has many bends, and wildlife, including elephants, deer and macaques, may appear on the road, so keep to the speed limit and give them room.

Weather follows the monsoon. From May to October, afternoons are wet and humid, and storms can be heavy. From November to February, mornings are cool and the air is clear. March to May is hot and dry. The best time for riding is the cool season, particularly in the early morning.

Fuel is easy, with stations along the highway and in town, and there are plenty of cafes, bakeries and restaurants. Stock up here before heading into the hills, where services are scarce.
t.asbyrgi@66.0,-16.5:
Ásbyrgi is a horseshoe-shaped canyon in the north-east of Iceland, about three and a half kilometres long and a kilometre wide, with vertical cliffs of around a hundred metres on three sides. The old story says it was made when Sleipnir, the eight-legged horse of Odin, put one hoof down on the earth, and from the air the shape does look like an enormous print. The scientific explanation is just as dramatic: catastrophic floods from the glacial river Jökulsá á Fjöllum carved it out in the aftermath of eruptions beneath the ice, in at least two huge episodes long before anyone lived here.

The floor of the canyon is a surprise. After the bleak lava plains and moorland you cross to get here, you step into a sheltered forest of birch, willow and spruce, with ferns and wild flowers underfoot and a small pond at the back, edged by dark cliffs. There is a campsite, a visitor centre and well-marked paths, and the rock island in the middle, called Eyjan, divides the canyon into two. Fulmars nest on the cliffs, and the air is full of birdsong in early summer. It is part of Vatnajökull National Park and the whole place feels protected, hushed and green.

The riding to get here is typical north Iceland. Route 85 is paved, with long straights, wide views and few turns, and you are often alone on the road for several minutes at a time. Crosswinds can be strong, especially along the coast, and the weather changes quickly, with fog and drizzle common even in July. A windproof layer is not optional. Gravel appears where tarmac ends, and loose stone can catch you out if you are going too fast.

Fuel is the main thing to plan. Services are sparse in this part of the country, and the larger town in the data is Húsavík, about thirty-eight kilometres away, which has pumps, shops and restaurants and is known for whale watching. Some small stations and a campsite shop may be open near the canyon in season, but you should not rely on them. Fill up in Húsavík or at the next village, and carry cash or a card with a chip and a PIN, since many pumps are unmanned.

Summer, from June to August, is the sensible time to come, with long days and open roads. In winter, many of the minor roads close.
t.dettifoss@65.8,-16.4:
Dettifoss is not the highest waterfall in Iceland, but it is the most powerful in Europe by volume, and standing next to it you quickly believe the claim. The glacial river Jökulsá á Fjöllum, grey with silt, tips over a rim about a hundred metres wide and drops some forty-five metres into a canyon, sending up a cloud of spray that hangs over the plateau and soaks anyone who gets too close. The noise is a constant roar, and the ground trembles slightly under your boots.

The country around it is a different sort of Iceland from the postcards. This is a high, stony desert of black basalt, moss and scree, with few trees and a wide sky. The river runs through a canyon cut into the rock, and a little way upstream and downstream there are two more falls, Selfoss and Hafragilsfoss, each with its own character. It was here that the opening scenes of the film Prometheus were shot, and it is easy to see why a film-maker would pick a place that looks like the start of the world.

Riding to Dettifoss involves a choice. The western approach, on route 862, is now paved and the easy option, with a smooth ride and big views over the plateau. The eastern side, on route 864, is a gravel road with potholes, washboard and loose stone that can be tricky on a road bike and demanding on any bike when it rains. It is also closed in winter. Check conditions with local information before you commit, and be careful of wind and fog, which can make the plateau a cold and disorienting place. Even in summer you will want a warm jacket.

The nearest pumps are around Mývatn to the west and in Húsavík to the north, so fill up before you go, and bring food and water if you can. A basic facility with a toilet is usually available at the car park, and in season there may be a small kiosk.

Stay on the marked paths, because the rocks are slippery and the drop is serious. The best time to come is a dry day in summer, when the light and the spray often make a rainbow across the canyon, and early or late hours keep the crowd to a minimum.
t.baikalsk@51.5,104.1:
Baikalsk has always lived with a famous neighbour. Lake Baikal, the deepest lake in the world at more than sixteen hundred metres, lies right at the end of the street, and behind the town the long, forested wall of the Khamar-Daban range rises close enough to feel in the weather. The town grew in the 1960s around a pulp and paper mill built on the shore, a decision that caused arguments about the lake's purity for decades before the mill finally closed in 2013. What was once an industrial site now feels like a place working out what it wants to be next.

The ride in from Slyudyanka, some thirty-four kilometres to the west, is one of the more relaxed ones on this side of the lake. The road keeps close to the foothills, passing through pine and birch forest with glimpses of grey-blue water between the trunks. The asphalt is generally fine, bends are moderate, and you meet logging trucks and the odd local in a hurry rather than crowds. Mornings are the best time, when the lake is calm and the light comes low over the water. In winter and early spring the wind and ice change everything, and snow can hold on in the hills well into spring.

With roughly fifteen thousand people, Baikalsk has everything a traveller needs: fuel, groceries, simple cafes and a few places to sleep. Slyudyanka, the nearest larger town, is the fallback if you want more choice. The shore itself is stony, the water cold even in August, and swimming is for the brave. Look for the fish, omul, smoked or salted, which is the lake's signature food and tastes best bought from a local seller rather than a roadside kiosk with a long queue.

Above the town there is a ski area that has made a modest name for itself on the slopes of the Khamar-Daban, and the mountain air in summer smells of cedar and warm resin. It is worth pausing to take in the scale of the thing. Baikal holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh water, and its seals, the nerpa, are found nowhere else. You will not see one from the road, but knowing they are out there makes the grey water look different.
t.kultuk@51.7,103.7:
Kultuk gave its name to a wind, and anyone who has crossed the southern end of Baikal on a bike will understand why. The village stands at the extreme southwestern tip of the lake, where the water narrows between the mountains, and when a strong westerly funnels down the basin the locals call it the kultuk. Gusts here can lean a loaded motorcycle sideways, so keep your speed steady and your grip loose when you leave the shelter of the trees.

It is also a place of junctions. The old Siberian trunk road and the Trans-Siberian Railway both swing past on their way around the lake, and the Tunkinsky Trakt, the route into the long valley between the Sayan mountains and the Khamar-Daban, starts nearby. Slyudyanka, a railway town of nearly nineteen thousand people about seven kilometres away, is where you will find fuel, shops and cafes in larger numbers; Kultuk itself is a village of four thousand with the basics and a handful of places to eat. The railway has a character of its own here, with the Circum-Baikal line, built in the early twentieth century with dozens of tunnels and stone bridges, running down the shore a short way east.

The ride out along the Tunkinsky Trakt is a pleasure. The road climbs gently into the valley with mountains on both sides, the asphalt is mostly good, and the corners are long and unhurried. Larch, pine and birch cover the slopes, and the light in late afternoon turns the hills a deep blue. In summer the meadows smell of cut grass, and in September the larches turn gold. Traffic is moderate, though trucks cluster on the climbs, so patience and a clear view are all you need to pass them safely.

Slyudyanka itself has a small mineral museum that recalls the marble and mica once quarried in the area, and the station building, faced with local stone, is worth a look if you have ten minutes. Buy water and food here, eat something hot, and top the tank before the valley, because the villages beyond are small. The Tunkinsky Trakt is long, so there is no point rushing the first hour.
t.mondy@51.7,101.0:
Mondy sits on the Irkut River at the western end of the Tunka valley, almost on the border with Mongolia, and it has the feel of a place at the end of something. The road from Arshan runs for hours along the valley floor between the Eastern Sayan on the north and the Khamar-Daban range on the south, and the farther you go, the fewer cars you share it with. By the time you arrive, the peaks have grown bare and sharp, and the air has that thin, cold edge of high country even in July.

The village itself is small and practical, a border settlement with a frontier post for the crossing into Mongolia. Fuel and food are basic, so fill up before the last stretch, and carry spare water and snacks in case a closed shop catches you out. Beyond the houses, the valley opens into pasture grazed by cattle and horses, and the sky seems bigger than it did lower down. Over the ridge to the north lies the Munku-Sardyk massif, the highest summit of the Eastern Sayan, rising above 3,400 metres and often snow-capped well into summer. You will not see its top from the road in poor weather, but when the cloud lifts, it dominates.

The riding, as far as the surface and the conditions go, is part of the charm. The main road is asphalt, with patches and frost heave that can bite after a hard winter, and the corners are gentle enough to let you watch the river. Morning light on the Irkut is clear and cold, afternoons bring wind, and thunderstorms can build over the mountains in July and August. Nights are cool even in summer, and a warm layer is not optional.

Buryat culture is strong in this valley, and you will see shrines and colourful prayer flags near springs and passes, a mixture of Buddhist and older shamanic practice that gives the landscape a quiet sacred quality. Hot springs are scattered through the Tunka valley, so it is worth asking locals about them. A visit here is less about a sight than about the sense of reaching an edge, of having ridden as far as the road allows before the frontier says stop.
t.pang sida national park@14.1,102.2:
Pang Sida is the eastern end of the great forest belt that stretches across north-eastern Thailand from Khao Yai to the Cambodian border, a block of jungle, waterfalls and rolling hills in Sa Kaeo province. Together with Khao Yai, Thap Lan, Ta Phraya and a wildlife sanctuary, it makes up the Dong Phayayen–Khao Yai Forest Complex, a World Heritage site that protects some of the best remaining monsoon forest in mainland South-east Asia.

It is less visited than Khao Yai, which is precisely its charm. The access roads from Sa Kaeo run through farmland, cassava and sugarcane fields before the forest closes in, and inside the park the road climbs gently past streams and viewpoints. The surface is generally good, but potholes, wandering dogs and sudden rain are part of the deal. The rainy season, from roughly May to October, brings the forest to life and fills the waterfalls, though it also makes the roads slick. In the cooler months from November to February the riding is most comfortable, and the mornings can even feel fresh. Remember that Thailand drives on the left.

The park is famous among nature lovers for its butterflies. In the rainy season, clouds of them gather at puddles along the roads and streams, yellow and white and sulphur-green, rising around you as you pass. Pang Sida Waterfall and several smaller falls tumble over sandstone ledges into pools. Elephants, gibbons, hornbills and deer live here, though the shy ones will hear you long before you see them. Listen for the whooping calls of gibbons in the early morning.

This border region carries layers of history. Not far east lies the frontier with Cambodia, crossed at Aranyaprathet, and the area saw refugee camps and fighting during the Khmer Rouge years and their aftermath. Today it is quiet farming country, and Sa Kaeo itself is a modest provincial town with markets, temples and some of the best som tam you can hope to find.

Fuel stations are plentiful along the main highways, and Sa Kaeo, about thirty kilometres away, has everything from fuel to repairs and simple hotels. Inside the park, facilities are basic: a visitor centre, camping and simple food. Carry water, a rain shell and insect repellent, and expect a small entrance fee.
t.dong yai wildlife sanctuary@14.2,102.6:
Near the Cambodian border, the forests of eastern Thailand are some of the wildest in the country, and Dong Yai is part of a great chain of them. The Dong Phayayen–Khao Yai forest complex, which UNESCO listed in 2005, covers about six thousand square kilometres of hills and valleys stretching from Khao Yai National Park to the Cambodian frontier. Dong Yai Wildlife Sanctuary is one of the five protected areas in the complex, together with Ta Phraya, Thap Lan and Pang Sida National Parks, and it forms a corridor for animals that need space.

The forest is home to elephants, gaur, sambar deer, leopards, and, though rarely seen, tigers, as well as Asian black bears, gibbons and an extraordinary range of birds, including several species of hornbill. This is one of the few places in Thailand where wild elephants still move in large numbers between protected areas. Most of the sanctuary has no public facilities, and access is limited, but the surrounding country gives a taste, with hills covered in dry evergreen and bamboo, and a thin population of farmers growing cassava, maize and rice.

For a rider, the roads in this part of eastern Thailand are typically smooth, well marked and quiet, with long straight sections and gentle rises. The famous road through Khao Yai National Park, to the west, is a winding mountain route with wildlife on the verges, and it is wise to ride slowly, since elephants and deer cross at night, and the park has strict speed limits. The cooler dry season, from November to February, is the best time for riding and wildlife watching, while the rainy season brings heavy showers and wet roads. In the border region, there are military checkpoints, and you should carry your passport and licence.

Soeng Sang, about twenty-eight kilometres away, is a small town with fuel, shops and noodle stalls, and the larger town of Pak Chong, on the Khao Yai road, has more choice. Thai roadside food is generally superb and cheap, and small stalls selling grilled chicken and sticky rice are often better than hotel restaurants. Carry water, wear a hat, and keep to marked roads, because the border area has landmines in places, as a legacy of old conflicts.
t.thap lan national park@14.2,102.1:
If Thailand has a forest that deserves the word primeval, it may well be around Thap Lan. The park lies in the south-east of the Khorat plateau, between the Sankamphaeng range and the lowlands, and it is one of the pieces of the Dong Phayayen–Khao Yai forest complex that UNESCO listed in 2005. The name is said to come from a type of palm that grows in the area, and the park is known for its rich lowland rainforest, rare in a country where so much has been cleared for farming.

It is a place of waterfalls, caves, rocky streams and tall trees, with a good chance of seeing wildlife if you have patience and a guide. Elephants, gaur and clouded leopards live here, and the park is part of the habitat of the Siamese crocodile and various hornbills, as well as hundreds of species of butterflies. Pang Sida, its neighbour, is known for its cascades and wide views from the escarpment. Most visitors come on guided walks and wildlife safaris, and it is best to arrange these in advance through the park office.

Getting there is part of the pleasure. Roads from Khon Buri and the main highway toward Prachinburi are well surfaced and mostly straight, but the last stretches into the park can be narrower, with sharp bends and the occasional herd of cows. Heavy rain in the wet season, from May to October, can cause flooding, and the dry season brings cooler air and clearer skies, though it is also hotter at midday than you might want. Wildlife on the road is a real hazard, especially at dusk, and snakes are often seen basking on the warm asphalt.

Khon Buri is the nearest town of any size and has fuel and food, though it is around thirty-five kilometres from the park. Within the park there is a small visitor centre and some simple food, but it is best to carry water and snacks. A local guide is the best way to understand what you are looking at, and to avoid the dangers of wandering alone in forest that can be hot, humid and easy to get lost in.
t.angkor@13.4,103.9:
Angkor is the great stone capital of the Khmer empire, spread across more than four hundred square kilometres of forest and rice field a few kilometres north of Siem Reap. The empire ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia between the ninth and the fifteenth centuries, and its kings built huge temples as symbols of the cosmos. Angkor Wat, built in the twelfth century by Suryavarman II and dedicated to Vishnu, is the largest religious monument in the world, with five towers rising like lotus buds above a vast moat. Its long walls carry carved reliefs of battles and myths, and it was later converted into a Buddhist temple that is still in use.

Not far away, Angkor Thom was the walled city of Jayavarman VII, with the enigmatic stone faces of the Bayon smiling from the towers. Ta Prohm, partly swallowed by giant silk-cotton and strangler fig trees, has been left as the French explorers found it, and it is the most atmospheric place in the whole complex. The monuments were forgotten by Europeans until the nineteenth century, though they were never really lost to the Cambodian people, and today they are the symbol of the nation, with Angkor Wat on the flag.

Visiting is a matter of planning. The heat is heavy, and a day among the stones means long walks and steep stairs, so water and a hat are essential. The most popular times are sunrise and sunset, with crowds in both places, and the quieter hours of mid-morning are better for smaller temples. A ticket is needed and is checked at barriers, and clothing that covers shoulders and knees is required at the main temples. The dry season, from November to February, is cooler and clearer, while the rainy months turn the moats green and the roads muddy.

The roads in Siem Reap province are flat and straight, with plenty of motorbikes, tuk-tuks, bicycles and trucks, and the rules are rather flexible. Be cautious at junctions and avoid riding after dark, when unlit vehicles are common. Siem Reap, a city of about a hundred and forty thousand, offers fuel, restaurants and every sort of lodging, and the local dish of fish amok, a mild curry steamed in banana leaf, is worth trying. The ride goes on to Koh Ker, a remote temple city far to the north-east, which is quiet and wild compared with the crowds of Angkor.
