t.roluos@13.3,104.0:
Roluos is where the story of Angkor begins. About thirteen kilometres south-east of Siem Reap, along the road toward Phnom Penh, a cluster of brick and sandstone temples marks Hariharalaya, the capital of the Khmer kings in the late ninth century. Before the great monuments of Angkor Wat and the Bayon were built, the rulers lived and built here, and the three main temples show the first mature forms of Khmer architecture. Preah Ko was dedicated in 879 by Indravarman I, and Bakong, a few years later, was the first great temple mountain, a stepped pyramid with elephants in stone at the corners, representing Mount Meru, the home of the gods.

Lolei, the third, stands on an island in what was once a huge reservoir, the Indratataka, and it was built by Indravarman's son, Yasovarman I, who later moved the capital to Angkor. The brickwork, the lintels and the carved figures at the doors are among the finest of the early period, and the buildings are much quieter than those of Angkor, since many tour groups skip them. In some places, monks still live in a modern monastery beside the old towers, and children play in the courtyards.

The countryside around is gentle and flat, with rice fields, sugar palms, ponds with lotus flowers and wooden houses on stilts. The light in the early morning and late afternoon turns the red brick glowing and the green fields bright. The heat is intense in the middle of the day, so a morning visit is wise. During the rainy season, from May to October, afternoon storms are frequent, and the dirt tracks between the temples turn to mud.

The road from Siem Reap is a busy national highway, with trucks, buses, tuk-tuks and motorbikes weaving among one another, so it is wise to stay alert and keep a safe distance. Once you turn off toward the temples, traffic becomes much calmer. Fuel is easy to find in Siem Reap, with stations on the highway, and simple drinks stalls near the temples sell cold coconuts and fruit. Stay a while, watch the sun sink over the palms, and think of the long Khmer story that began here, a few kilometres from the place where the biggest monument was later raised.
t.teide national park@28.3,-16.6:
Spain's highest mountain is a volcano standing in the middle of an island in the Atlantic, and that alone makes Teide worth the ride. It rises to 3,715 metres above sea level, and from the ocean floor it is one of the tallest volcanic structures on Earth. The national park around it, listed by UNESCO in 2007, is a high desert of pumice, lava and strange rock towers, set in an ancient caldera, the Cañadas, and the road across it is among the most extraordinary on any motorcycle map. The Roques de García, a cluster of twisted, wind-carved pillars, stand in front of the mountain like a stage set.

The ascent is the main event. Whichever side you climb from, the road leaves the green, humid slopes and enters pine forest, then breaks above the clouds into a bare, orange-brown landscape where the air is thin and dry. Bends are broad and well graded, but the road can be busy with tour buses and rental cars, especially around midday, so an early start is best. Weather can change quickly, with wind, cold and even snow in winter, which can close the road, so check conditions before you go. In May and June the slopes bloom with the tall, red-flowering tajinaste, an endemic plant that looks like a rocket.

La Guancha and Vilaflor, with five thousand and two thousand people respectively, are small, and the better choice is one of the bigger coastal towns. Vilaflor is one of the highest villages in Spain, at about 1,400 metres. A parador, a state-run hotel, stands near the base of the cable car, and a cafe there offers a hot drink with a view.

Remember that the park is strictly protected, so do not take stones or sand, and keep to the marked paths. At night the sky is so clear that the observatories on the slopes are among the best in the world. If you can, stay for sunset, when the whole mountain turns pink, then violet, then black.
t.temple of preah vihear@14.4,104.7:
The Temple of Preah Vihear is a Khmer sanctuary built on the lip of the Dângrêk escarpment, the long sandstone wall that separates the Cambodian plain from the Thai plateau. The coordinates given here sit on the Thai side, about twenty-eight kilometres from Kantharalak, which is the nearest sizeable town and the place to fill the tank and the stomach before you head up. The temple itself is Cambodian, dedicated to Shiva, and its builders, working over several centuries from the ninth century onward, laid it out as a long axis climbing from the plain to the cliff edge instead of the usual compact tower on a square.

That axis is what makes it special. You pass through a succession of gopuras and causeways, each higher than the last, and at the end the stone floor simply stops above a drop of several hundred metres, with Cambodia's forests spread out below. The sandstone carvings, lintels with Vishnu and the churning of the ocean among them, are worn and warm to the touch. The temple was the subject of a long dispute between Thailand and Cambodia, taken to the International Court of Justice in 1962 and again later, and the border area has had tense moments since. Check current access rules before you ride up, because crossing points and permissions have changed more than once.

The approach on the Thai side is a proper mountain road, climbing through dry dipterocarp forest in steady bends with short, steep pitches. The surface is generally good tarmac, but heavy rain loosens gravel on the corners and the mist can sit on the escarpment in the cool months. Early morning is the right time, when the air is clear and the haze has not yet blurred the plain. Traffic is light apart from weekend tour buses.

Practicalities are simple. There are food stalls and drink sellers near the car parks, and Thai highway stations are plentiful on the main routes, but not on the climb, so take fuel in Kantharalak. Bring water, a hat, and shoes with grip, since the stone steps are polished and the walk to the cliff edge is longer than it looks. Keep to marked paths, as the area has had unexploded ordnance from past conflicts, and treat any no-go sign as a hard rule.
t.angkor@13.4,103.8:
Angkor is bigger than most visitors expect, and its scale only starts to make sense once you realise that it was a city, not a temple. The great complex north of Siem Reap, in north-western Cambodia, was the capital of the Khmer Empire from the ninth century to the fifteenth, and at its height it covered hundreds of square kilometres, with reservoirs, canals, roads and houses of wood that have long since vanished. What survives is the stone: Angkor Wat, built in the early twelfth century by King Suryavarman II as a temple to Vishnu, with its five towers, long galleries of carved relief and a moat that mirrors the sunrise, and Angkor Thom, the walled city built by Jayavarman VII, with the Bayon and its dozens of towers carved with huge, smiling faces.

The jungle played its part, too. At Ta Prohm, silk-cotton and strangler fig trees grow over the roofs and walls, their roots pouring over the stones like melted wax, and the place has a hushed, green stillness that few other sites match. The complex was listed as a World Heritage site in 1992. Sunrise at Angkor Wat draws large crowds, so go to a quieter temple at dawn, and visit the main ones at midday, when many people retreat to lunch and the heat is fierce.

For riders, the situation is changeable. A pass, bought at the ticket office, is needed for entry to the park, and rules for foreign visitors on motorcycles and scooters have changed several times in recent years, so ask locally before you hire or ride anything. The roads between the temples are flat and smooth, shaded by tall trees, and the traffic is slow, with tuk-tuks, bicycles and tour buses. The ride on to Koh Ker, the tenth-century capital far to the north-east, with its stepped pyramid, takes you out of the tourist zone onto the main road, past rice fields, palm trees and stilted houses, with good tarmac and lots of children waving.

Siem Reap, eight kilometres away, is a lively town of well over a hundred thousand people, with fuel stations, restaurants, markets and every kind of hotel, so stock up there. The best time is the cool dry season, from November to February, while the hot months of March to May can be oppressive, and the rains from June to October bring heavy showers and green rice fields. Try amok, the fish curry steamed in banana leaf, and fresh coconut water from a roadside stall.
t.dawson city@64.1,-139.4:
Dawson City was built on a gamble. In August 1896, gold was found in a creek flowing into the Klondike river, and within two years, more than thirty thousand people had come to the swampy flat at the river's mouth, having crossed mountain passes with tons of supplies, floated down the Yukon, and spent everything they had. Most got no gold. A few got rich overnight, and the town rose, with saloons, theatres, hotels and dance halls, to become the largest city north of Seattle and west of Winnipeg.

Writers and chroniclers made the place famous. Jack London spent a winter in a cabin near here, and Robert Service, a bank clerk, wrote his ballads about the gold rush while living in town. Today the wooden false-front buildings of Front Street, restored by Parks Canada, still give the place a feeling of the past, with boardwalks along the dirt streets and a casino that keeps the gambling hall tradition alive. A local drink called the Sourtoe Cocktail, which includes a preserved human toe, is a famous party trick that you may or may not want to try.

The setting is dramatic. The Yukon River, broad, silty and fast, flows past the town below a steep slope of loose rock called the Midnight Dome, and in summer, the sun barely sets. Winters are long and dark, with temperatures of minus forty. The ground is permafrost, so some of the old buildings lean at odd angles.

For riders, Dawson is the starting point of the Top of the World Highway, which climbs out of the Yukon valley along a ridge toward Alaska. A small cable ferry carries vehicles across the Yukon river free of charge in summer, and the road on the other side is partly paved and partly gravel, with big views. Fuel is available in town, and you should fill up before heading out, since there is none for a long way. The border at Poker Creek is open only in summer. Check weather, carry spare supplies, and expect mosquitoes.
t.mount qingcheng and the dujiangyan irrig:
The Min River comes down out of the Tibetan edge of Sichuan in a hurry, and the Chengdu plain below it would have flooded every year if a governor named Li Bing had not worked out how to tame it in the third century BC. His Dujiangyan scheme, begun around 256 BC, splits the river with a man-made island and a cut through the hillside, sending the surplus to the sea and the rest into canals that water the plain. It still works, more than two thousand years later, which is the real wonder of it, and it is the reason Sichuan became known as the land of abundance.

You walk out over suspension bridges and look down on the water as it boils and divides. The sound of the river is a constant, and the sight of anglers and old men on the quay gives the place an everyday feel that is easy to forget amid the tourist crowds. Mount Qingcheng, a few kilometres away, is a different thing, a wooded hill covered in Daoist temples, traditionally the birthplace of the Daoist religion in its organised form, with stone steps, tea houses and bamboo thickets.

Riding up from Chengdu you travel a fast, well-surfaced road across the plain, often busy with trucks, and then the country starts to lift. The road to the Wolong panda reserve, which this stop shares a ride with, climbs along the river into forested mountains, and it is still marked by the effects of the 2008 earthquake, with rebuilt bridges and tunnels and fresh retaining walls. Corners are more frequent as you climb, and rain, mist and rockfall are all real possibilities, so check conditions before you go.

Fill the tank down on the plain, because the towns up in the valleys are smaller and services thinner. Tianpeng, the nearest sizeable place, has what you need. Local food is Sichuan food at its best: hotpot, mapo tofu, and the tea of the Qingcheng hills, served in the old tea houses where nobody will hurry you.

Spring and autumn are the best times, because summers are hot and humid and winters are damp and grey. Tickets and entrance are in the usual Chinese pattern, with a lot of walking involved, so wear shoes rather than riding boots if you can.
t.garajonay national park@28.1,-17.2:
Mist is the main character in this forest. On La Gomera, one of the smallest of the Canary Islands, the trade winds blow clouds against the mountains in the centre of the island, and the trees comb the moisture out of the air so effectively that a damp forest stays damp all year. The Garajonay National Park, which covers the high ground at around 1,400 metres, is one of the best remaining stands of laurisilva, a type of subtropical cloud forest that once covered much of southern Europe before the ice ages. Moss hangs from the branches, lichen covers the trunks, and the light has a green, underwater quality. UNESCO listed the park in 1986.

Garajonay takes its name from a legend. Gara, the daughter of the lord of one island district, fell in love with Jonay, a young man from Tenerife, whose island is visible across the water on a clear day. Their families forbade the match, and the lovers, so the story goes, died together on a skewer of cedar wood at the highest point. The summit, at 1,487 metres, is the island's highest, and you can walk to it from the road in a few minutes.

Riding on La Gomera is spectacular and demanding. The island is a rounded volcanic cone cut by deep ravines called barrancos, and the roads descend into them in long hairpin sequences and climb out the other side. Surfaces are generally good but narrow, and tour buses on the main road make blind corners something to respect. On the high ground the weather changes in minutes, from sun to dense fog and drizzle, so carry waterproofs even if the forecast is good. In 2012 a large fire burned part of the park, which has since been regenerating.

For fuel, San Sebastián de La Gomera, the capital, thirteen kilometres away, has the main stations, and a few villages such as Vallehermosa have pumps. The local food is simple and good, with a honey made from palm sap, goat cheese, potatoes with a red spicy sauce called mojo, and a whistled language called Silbo Gomero that islanders used for centuries to talk across the ravines, which UNESCO has also recognised.
t.myvatn@65.6,-17.0:
Mývatn means midge lake, and the name is honest, because in early summer clouds of small, harmless flies hang above the water and rise from the shore in a shimmering haze. They are the foundation of an ecosystem that feeds one of the richest populations of breeding ducks in Europe, and in June the lake is crowded with them. Bring a face cover in still weather, and keep your visor closed.

The landscape is the real reason to come. Mývatn sits on the volcanic rift that splits Iceland, and everything around it is the result of fire: the Skútustaðagígar pseudocraters, rings of grassy cones formed when lava flowed over wet ground and blasted steam through it; the labyrinth of black lava pillars and arches at Dimmuborgir; the perfect tuff crater Hverfjall, a kilometre across and easy to climb. East of the lake, the Ring Road climbs the Námaskarð pass through Hverir, a rust-coloured geothermal field where mud pots plop and steam hisses out of vents, and the whole place smells strongly of sulphur. The nearby Krafla volcano erupted repeatedly between 1975 and 1984, and a walk across its blackened lava field is a humbling experience.

Riding here is easy but not entirely relaxed. The Ring Road, Route 1, is paved and well maintained, with long straights and gentle curves across open lava plains and moorland. The risks are wind, which can turn violent and push a bike sideways, sudden rain and fog, and gravel on the verges and at junctions. Traffic is moderate in summer. The best time is June to August, with the midnight sun in June giving light all night, and by September snow can arrive. Fuel is available in Reykjahlíð, the village on the lake's northeast shore, and the next bigger service stops are at Akureyri in one direction and Egilsstaðir in the other. Laugar, about twenty kilometres away, is the nearest settlement of any size to the west.

Locals bake rye bread in the hot ground near the lake and serve it with smoked trout, which is worth trying, and the Mývatn Nature Baths, a geothermal lagoon of milky blue water, are an ideal place to soak after a cold, windy day. Dress warmly, even in summer, because temperatures at the lake can drop sharply.
t.ayutthaya river easy ride@13.9,100.7:
The Rangsit canal, dug in the 1890s to open the plain north of Bangkok to rice farming, runs straight as a ruler across the flatlands, and these coordinates fall just south of it, near Khlong Luang, in the ever-expanding northern suburbs. The land here was once all paddy fields, and the canal system, built by a company owned by the king and a group of investors, turned a swamp into the richest rice land in the country. Today the fields are shrinking before warehouses, universities and housing estates, but the canals remain, and their banks are lined with temples, shrines and old wooden houses.

Don Mueang, the old airport, lies a few kilometres to the south, and Thammasat University's Rangsit campus sits to the north. A large Buddhist temple at Khlong Luang draws crowds on festival days, and its vast complex of halls and gardens is one of the largest in the country. Visitors should dress modestly and be respectful, and photography is restricted in some areas.

Ayutthaya, the old capital, lies about forty kilometres to the north, and the ride that sets out from here is an easy day trip along the river. The road is Highway 1, the main road to the north, which is wide, fast and busy with traffic, and a better option is the quieter road that runs beside the river, with temples, boatyards and old houses. The surface is good, the bends are gentle, and the river is nearly always in sight. Start early to beat the heat and the crowds, and leave time for the ruins.

Fuel is no problem. Ban Lam Luk Ka, a town of sixty thousand people, is crowded with stations, malls and restaurants, and Khlong Luang, with over a hundred and eighteen thousand, has even more. Pathum Thani is a smaller place with a good market. In the cool season, from November to February, the weather is mild and the sky is clear, and the riding is a pleasure. In the hot season, the heat is brutal, and by midday the roads shimmer. Pack water, sunscreen and a rain jacket, and start before the sun is high.
Bangkok sits on a river delta that was seabed not very long ago in geological terms, and these coordinates, in Bang Bo district south-east of the city, show it plainly. The ground here lies only a metre or two above the tide, so a high point in the usual rider's sense does not exist. The highest things on the horizon are the golden finials of temples, the gantries of container yards and the flyovers that carry the Bangna-Trat highway over the canals, and the closest thing to a summit is the crest of one of those concrete ramps.

The national park here, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, covers a landscape of lava flows, pumice fields and strange rock formations, with a flora of its own, including the Teide viper's bugloss, a tall spike of red flowers that blooms in late spring. The ride from the north is the best way in. The road from La Orotava climbs steadily through pine forest in broad bends, then reaches a long straight over the pass, with the volcano ahead. It continues across the caldera floor through a landscape that looks like another planet, with colours ranging from black and red to yellow and white. The surface is excellent, the road is wide, and the traffic is steady. Wind and cold at this altitude are real: temperatures can drop below freezing at night even in summer, and snow closes the road occasionally in winter. Cloud often lies below the pass, and the transition from the grey sea of cloud to the clear blue sky above is dramatic.

Fill the tank in La Orotava or Los Realejos before you start, because the next reliable stations are on the other side of the island. A café and small restaurant at the pass serves hot food, and a few picnic areas are scattered through the pine forest below.

Go early, since the afternoon cloud often rises and hides the cone.
t.teide cable car@28.3,-16.6:
The cable car lifts you from 2,356 metres to 3,555 metres in about eight minutes, which is a very short time to change planet. At the lower station, the air is clear and cold, and the ground is a mass of dark lava and pale pumice. At the top, in thin air and a sharper wind, you are almost at the summit of Teide and standing above the clouds, with a view that on a clear day takes in the other Canary Islands floating on the sea. The car holds a few dozen people and runs back and forth through the day, weather permitting.

Practical points matter here. Tickets are in demand and queues can be long, so booking in advance online is wise, particularly in high season. The cable car may be suspended without notice if wind is strong, and the altitude can cause headaches or breathlessness, especially if you have come straight from the coast, so go gently and drink water. Walking from the top station to the actual summit, a further stretch of about two hundred metres of ascent, requires a free permit from the park authority, which is limited in number and must be arranged ahead of time.

The road to the base station, the TF-21, crosses Las Cañadas, the high plateau inside the old caldera, and it is one of the most spectacular drives in Spain. It passes the Roques de García, a cluster of weathered rock towers beside a flat plain of ash, and the Parador, the only hotel inside the park, set against the cone. The surface is smooth, the bends are long and open, and the air smells of resin and dust. In winter, snow may close sections of the road, and ice can form on shaded corners.

The nearest villages are Vilaflor, on the south side, which has a few services, and La Orotava or Los Realejos on the north, which have everything you need. Fill up before you go, as the climb uses more fuel than you expect. A café at the lower station serves coffee and snacks, but prices are high, and it is worth bringing water.

A midweek morning offers the best chance of clear skies and short queues.
t.boca tauce@28.2,-16.7:
Boca Tauce is where the south road into Teide National Park meets the one that cuts across the caldera, a junction sitting a little over two thousand metres up on Tenerife's volcanic spine. There is no village, just tarmac, pale pumice, and the rust-coloured Roques de García standing off to the east like a row of melted candles. The mountain itself, Teide, rises behind them to 3,718 metres, the highest point in Spain, and on a clear morning it looks close enough to hit with a thrown helmet.

The ride up is a slow education in how a landscape changes. From Vilaflor the TF-21 climbs through Canary pine forest, long-needled trees that survive fire by sprouting from the bark, and then the trees give out and you are in a different planet. The surface is generally good, the corners open and rhythmic rather than tight, and the air thins enough that the bike feels a touch lazier on the straights. Weekends bring coaches and rental cars crawling to the viewpoints, so go early or late. In winter this is a genuine mountain: snow and ice can close or slow the road, and it is properly cold when the coast below is in T-shirt weather. Dress for the altitude, not the beach.

The ground here is the floor of Las Cañadas, a vast collapsed caldera ringed by cliffs, with Teide built up inside it by later eruptions. Black lava fields, stands of golden retama broom that flower in late spring, and a silence that carries. The Guanches, Tenerife's original inhabitants, considered the mountain a place where the devil lived, and standing among the lava you can see why. The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the lack of light pollution makes the night sky famously clear.

Plan fuel before you climb. There is nothing in the park, and Vilaflor is small, so the safer move is to fill up in Guía de Isora or Adeje on the way. Water, coffee and a basic lunch can be had at the Parador and the visitor facilities a few kilometres along, at tourist prices. Come down the same way you came or follow the TF-38 towards Santiago del Teide, a quieter descent with views toward La Gomera on a good day.
t.irkutsk@52.3,104.3:
Irkutsk was a Siberian trading post that became a city of merchants, exiles and gold, and it has an air of faded elegance that surprises people who expect only snow and railways. It stands on the Angara river, the only outlet of Lake Baikal, about seventy kilometres downstream from the lake, and it was founded in 1661 as a fort. Fur traders, tea merchants and gold dealers made fortunes here, and the grand wooden houses with carved window frames, known as wooden lace, still line some of the old streets, leaning a little as the ground shifts.

Irkutsk was also a place of exile, and the Decembrists, aristocratic officers who had rebelled against the tsar in 1825, were sent here, bringing with them books, music and manners. Their houses, now museums, are among the city's best-known sights, and the city was long known as the Paris of Siberia, an exaggeration but a charming one. The Trans-Siberian railway arrived in 1898, and the big station is still a landmark. Soviet housing, wide avenues and modern shopping centres fill the newer districts, with a long riverside promenade along the Angara.

For riders, Irkutsk is the starting point for Baikal, the deepest and oldest lake in the world, holding about a fifth of the planet's unfrozen fresh water. The road to Listvyanka, a lakeside village, winds through hills and forest for around seventy kilometres, with a good surface and fair traffic, though weekends are busy. Farther south, the old Circum-Baikal route and the coast road toward Slyudyanka and Baikalsk pass between steep wooded slopes and the clear blue water, with mountains rising on the far shore. The water is cold enough to take your breath away, even in August.

The weather is continental, with hot summers, cold winters of minus twenty or lower, and sudden storms. Wind on the lake can be strong, and fog and rain are common in late summer. The best season is June to September, with a short, golden autumn.

Irkutsk has all the services of a big city, with fuel at many stations, repairs, supermarkets and hotels. Beyond the city, villages have small stations, but they are spaced apart, so fill the tank before leaving. Try omul, a smoked or salted fish from Baikal, sold at stalls in Listvyanka, and drink hot tea afterward. Mosquitoes can be fierce in the forests in early summer.
t.vilaflor@28.2,-16.6:
Vilaflor lies on the southern slope of Tenerife at about 1,400 metres, and it is generally described as the highest village in Spain. The air up here is cool and thin, and the landscape is a mix of terraced fields, almond and pear trees, and the dark, scented forest of Canary pine that cloaks the mountain above. Below, the land falls away in long folds to a sea that is often hidden by a layer of cloud. It is a small, whitewashed place of just under two thousand people, with a church, a plaza and a long reputation for garlic.

The village is also associated with Saint Peter Claver, a Jesuit missionary born in Catalonia who spent his life working among enslaved Africans in Colombia, and who is said to have lived in Vilaflor early in his career. A statue stands in the square. Above the village, the road climbs into the Teide National Park, where the great volcano Mount Teide, at about 3,700 metres the highest peak in Spain, dominates a lunar landscape of lava fields, pumice and rock pinnacles. The Roques de García, a cluster of bizarre rock formations, stand beside the road and are a classic photo stop.

The riding on the Teide road is superb. It climbs in long, graceful bends through the pine forest, past viewpoints over the clouds, and then emerges onto an open plateau, with the volcano's bulk filling the sky. Air thins, engine power drops, and the temperature can fall by fifteen degrees compared with the coast. In winter, snow can close the road, and fog and strong winds are common. In summer, the road is busy with tourist buses, so early morning is best.

There are a couple of simple restaurants in the village, serving rabbit in salmorejo, goat stew and wrinkled potatoes with spicy mojo sauce.

The sunsets above the clouds are extraordinary, and at night the sky is so clear that the national park is a recognised stargazing site.
t.slyudyanka@51.7,103.7:
Slyudyanka sits at the southern tip of Lake Baikal, where the old railway turns the corner of the world's deepest lake, and the whole town carries the feel of a railway place. The name comes from slyuda, the Russian word for mica, which was mined in the hills behind the town for centuries and used for windows and later for electrical insulation. The mica pits and the quarries that supplied marble to the rest of the country shaped the town, and the stones around here are a collector's dream, with many kinds of crystals and minerals.

The railway station is the unmissable monument. It is the only station in Russia built entirely of marble, using the local white and grey stone, and it dates from the years when the Circum-Baikal line was being laid, among the most expensive stretches of the Trans-Siberian. The railway squeezed along the cliffs of the lake's southern shore with dozens of tunnels, bridges and retaining walls built in stone, and a trip along it by train or on foot is an experience in itself. The old route is a heritage line today, and you can still find old stone portals of tunnels in the forest.

Baikal itself is on another scale. It holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh water, it is more than 1,600 metres deep at its deepest, and it is thought to be twenty-five million years old. The water is so clear that you can see far down, and the shores here are lined with pebbles, rocky headlands and coniferous forest. The lake is cold even in August, and the swimming is bracing. In winter, it freezes to a thick layer of transparent ice that can carry vehicles, a spectacle of cracks and bubbles.

From Slyudyanka, roads lead west along the Tunkinsky valley toward Arshan, a village at the foot of the Sayan Mountains with mineral springs, and east along the lake toward Baikalsk. The roads are generally decent, with long straights and some gentle curves, and the mountains of the Khamar-Daban range rise behind. In summer, trucks and tourist traffic are heavy on the main highway, and potholes appear in spring.

Slyudyanka has fuel stations, shops and cafés. The famous local fish is omul, a type of lake whitefish, which is smoked or salted and sold by roadside vendors, and it is delicious with bread and a hot cup of tea. The best months are June to September, and by October the cold has returned.
t.la laguna@28.5,-16.3:
La Laguna looks like a city that was planned on paper, because it was. Founded in the late fifteenth century after the Spanish conquest of Tenerife, it was laid out on a grid without fortifications and became a model for colonial towns in the Americas. UNESCO listed the old centre in 1999, and the pastel houses, wooden balconies and tiled patios make a pleasant half-hour on foot. The university here is among the oldest in the Canaries, and the student crowd keeps the cafes busy.

The setting is the thing to understand. La Laguna sits about 550 metres above sea level on a fertile plain, in the trade-wind belt, so clouds roll over it on many days and the air is cooler and damper than on the south coast. Seen from the road, the whole Anaga massif rises behind it, covered in laurel forest that is a relic of subtropical woodland once spread around the Mediterranean. Locals will tell you the city has its own weather, and they are right. A rain jacket stays in the top box.

The airport called Los Rodeos, now Tenerife North, lies in the municipality, and it is the site of the 1977 runway collision between two jumbo jets in fog, the worst accident in aviation history. Fog is the point worth remembering as a rider as well: when the cloud comes down on the plateau, visibility can fall quickly, so slow down and put your lights on.

For riding, La Laguna is the start of two very different days. West and south, the TF-24 and the roads through the pine forest climb toward Mount Teide, at 3,715 metres the highest peak in Spain, with its landscapes of lava fields and pale volcanic scree. Northeast, the narrow roads into Anaga twist through villages and ridges with hairpins and blind corners. Surface quality is mostly good, but cloud, wet leaves and rock fall can interrupt the flow. Early morning is calm. Afternoon traffic around Santa Cruz is dense.

Practically, with a population of over a hundred and fifty thousand, there is fuel everywhere, cafes in every square, and the sweet, strong barraquito coffee that is a Tenerife habit. The tram links to Santa Cruz, which makes a good spot to leave luggage or keep a bike overnight.
t.khao yai@13.9,100.5:
Pak Kret is a town of potters. North of Bangkok, on the Chao Phraya, the red-brown clay of the riverbank has been fired into earthenware here since the Mon people settled the area in the eighteenth century, and the tradition continues on a small island called Koh Kret, reached by a short ferry. Walking the narrow concrete lanes around the island with the sound of kilns and the sight of rows of terracotta pots drying in the sun is a good reason to come. Pak Kret itself is a busy suburban town of nearly two hundred thousand, and it is close to the pin.

The neighbouring province of Nonthaburi has another claim to fame, its durians, which are prized across Thailand. In the season, from April to June, roadside stalls sell the fruit in heaps, and the smell hangs in the warm air. The Chao Phraya here is wide and brown, busy with tugs, barges and long-tail boats, and the banks are lined with temples and old wooden houses.

For a rider, the roads in this area are mostly urban and slow. Chaeng Watthana and Tiwanon roads carry heavy traffic, and the combination of motorbikes, vans, buses and pedestrians requires constant attention. Some of the quieter lanes beside canals are more pleasant, with temples and market stalls to pass, but they can be narrow and potholed. Floods in the rainy season are common, and dusk brings clouds of mosquitoes. Early mornings, before the heat and commuter jams, are cooler and calmer. Parking for bikes is easy near the ferry pier.

Practically, everything is available. Fuel stations are along every main road, shopping malls sell supplies and spares, and there are food courts and street stalls serving noodles, grilled meat and sweet snacks. The ferry to Koh Kret is cheap and runs frequently, and bikes are usually carried at a small charge, though the island is best explored on foot or by hired bicycle. Bring cash, because small vendors rarely take cards. Weekends bring crowds from the city, so visit on a weekday if possible. The real Khao Yai lies far to the north-east, but this stop is an easy and rewarding contrast.
t.phnom penh@11.6,104.9:
Phnom Penh sits where three great rivers meet, the Mekong, the Tonle Sap and the Bassac, and the confluence is known in Khmer as Chaktomuk, the four faces. The city is Cambodia's capital and by far its biggest, with about one and a half million people, and it has an energy that arrives in stages: first the heat, then the noise, then the smell of charcoal smoke, frangipani and river mud. The riverfront promenade at dusk, with families on the pavement, food carts and the golden roofs of the Royal Palace, is one of the great evenings of Southeast Asia.

The name comes from a legend about a woman called Penh, who found four Buddha statues in a tree trunk floating in the river and built a hill, Wat Phnom, to house them in the fourteenth century. The French made the city their colonial capital, and leafy boulevards and yellow villas from that time survive among the temples. The Royal Palace and the Silver Pagoda, with its floor of silver tiles, are the main sights, and the National Museum holds a fine collection of Khmer sculpture from Angkor and earlier.

The city also holds one of the darkest chapters of the twentieth century. Between 1975 and 1979 the Khmer Rouge emptied Phnom Penh and then ran a regime in which about a quarter of the population died, and the memorial sites, including Tuol Sleng and the Choeung Ek killing fields, are visited with a mixture of respect and sorrow. The ride that starts here continues to a lesser-known site connected to that history, and it is best approached quietly.

Riding in Phnom Penh is a challenge that requires adaptation. Traffic drives on the right, but the rules are loose, motorbikes move like shoals of fish, and everything happens at once at intersections. Go slowly, watch the flow, avoid peak hours, and expect to be tooted at constantly, which is more a greeting than a warning. Fuel is available at stations on every main road, and there is excellent food, from noodle soups to grilled fish by the river. Carry water, as the heat is heavy for most of the year.
t.cambodian memorial sites from centres of:
West of Phnom Penh, the flat rice plain begins to roll into low hills, and the land of Kampong Speu opens out in a scatter of sugar palms, small farms and monasteries. This is the province of palm sugar, tapped from the toddy palms by climbers who go up the trunks twice a day, and the roadsides are lined with stalls selling blocks of it, along with fresh coconuts and fruit. The region is quiet and rural, with a way of life that has hardly changed in decades, and the sense of a different Cambodia from the capital's crowds.

The memorial sites that the ride seeks out in this area are part of a recent UNESCO listing of Cambodian places of memory, which includes Tuol Sleng, Choeung Ek and a small site at M-13. The latter was an early Khmer Rouge prison in the forest, where the man later known as Duch ran a security centre from 1971, before he moved to the notorious S-21 in Phnom Penh. Visits to such sites call for quiet and respect. The aim of the listing is to preserve these places so that the story is told truthfully, and to honour the dead.

The road west from the capital, National Highway 4, is wide and busy with trucks bound for the port of Sihanoukville, and the side roads that branch off toward villages and temples are narrower and rougher, with potholes and sudden stretches of red dust. Dogs, cattle and children on bicycles share the surface, and in the rainy season, from May to October, puddles hide holes. The best months for riding are November to February, when the air is drier and cooler.

Kampong Speu, a provincial town of over thirty thousand people thirty-eight kilometres away, has fuel, simple restaurants and guesthouses, and it is the sensible place to fill up and eat. Out in the countryside you will find roadside shops that sell petrol in bottles, which is fine in an emergency, but do not rely on it. Carry water and a rain jacket, and plan to return before dusk, since lighting on the rural roads is poor.
t.listvyanka@51.9,104.9:
Listvyanka is the small lakeside village where the Angara River leaves Lake Baikal, and the first place most visitors see the great lake. Baikal is the deepest lake on Earth and holds roughly a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh water, which is a fact people repeat constantly because it stays astonishing. The village lies about seventy kilometres from Irkutsk, along a road that follows the Angara, with Bolshaya Rechka a few kilometres up the shore.

The road from Irkutsk is quick and mostly well surfaced, climbing out of the Angara valley through pine and larch forest, with open bends and short straights. It is also busy: on weekends and in summer, traffic can be heavy, with tour buses and local cars, and the final approach into the village is slow. The best times are early morning and weekdays, or the shoulder seasons, when the forest turns gold in September and the lake mists hang in the air. In winter the lake freezes into clear blue ice, but the road can be slippery.

Listvyanka is a tourist village in the best and worst senses. It has a long lakeshore lined with cafes, souvenir stalls and guesthouses, and the main attraction is the market on the waterfront, where women sell smoked omul, the local whitefish, wrapped in paper and still warm. The Baikal Limnological Museum, which has an aquarium of local species, including the freshwater Baikal seal, the nerpa, is worth an hour. Nearby is the Shaman Stone at the source of the Angara, a rock that local legend says was thrown by Baikal in anger at his daughter's elopement with the river. The village's name comes from the larch, listvennitsa, which grows on the hills.

Nature is the real reason to come. The lake water is cold, clear and deep, the forest smells of resin and wet stone, and the hills behind the village are lined with trails, including one up to a viewpoint known as Chersky Stone, named after a Polish geologist who studied the lake. Baikal's endemic species number in the thousands, and the whole lake is listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage site.

Buy fuel in Irkutsk, since options in the village are limited and prices higher. Food is good and plentiful, and rooms fill early in summer.
t.arshan@51.9,102.4:
Arshan means healing water in Buryat, and the village earns its name. It sits near the head of the Tunka valley, a long, flat-bottomed trough running east to west between the Eastern Sayan mountains to the north and the Tunka Alps to the south, and it has been a spa resort for well over a century. The nearest larger settlement is Kyren, about thirty kilometres away, with Zhemchug a small neighbour; fuel stations are in Kyren and along the valley road, so fill the tank before heading up toward the Mondy road.

Getting here is a pleasure. The Tunkinsky Trakt comes from Kultuk at the southern tip of Lake Baikal and climbs through pine and larch forest, then opens onto the valley, a wide green bowl of meadows, birch groves and farms, with white-capped peaks standing along the skyline on both sides. The road is mostly decent tarmac, with long easy bends and straights, and traffic is moderate. Summer weekends can be busy with holidaymakers, and spring brings high water in the rivers. From Arshan, the road to Mondy climbs toward the Mongolian border, with the highest summits of the Eastern Sayan rising above three thousand metres.

The Tunka valley is a meeting place of Buryat and Russian culture. Buddhist prayer flags, small shrines and the occasional stupa mark the Buryat presence, and in several places stones carry painted prayers. Spa houses and sanatoria stand in the village among pine trees, with mineral springs that people drink and bathe in, and the smell of sulphur is not unknown. A small waterfall and a mountain stream run just behind the village, where a short walk takes you into dense forest of cedar and fir.

The surrounding nature is strongly alpine. The Tunka Alps and Sayan ridges hold glaciers, high lakes and rocky summits, and the valley itself has hot springs scattered along its length. Hawks and eagles are easy to spot, and the forests hold deer and bears. The valley air is dry and bright, with a cool edge even in summer.

Plan to arrive in the afternoon, eat something simple, take a soak if you feel like it, and start early for the mountain road. Keep a warm layer on hand, since the weather changes quickly.
t.maspalomas@27.8,-15.6:
Maspalomas is two things that do not quite match: a resort town of about thirty thousand people, and a nature reserve of dunes the size of a small desert. The dunes stretch for several kilometres along the south coast of Gran Canaria, a shifting sea of golden sand blown from the Atlantic, with a palm oasis at one end and a lighthouse, built in 1890, at the other. Camel rides carry visitors across the sand, the wind sculpts new ridges every day, and at sunrise or sunset the shadows are long and dramatic. The reserve protects a rare ecosystem, and walkers are asked to keep to marked paths.

The resort is about sun, and it works efficiently: hotels, apartment blocks, shopping centres and miles of beach, with Playa del Inglés immediately next door. The climate is a big part of the draw, with temperatures that rarely fall below eighteen degrees even in winter and a sky that is often cloudless. It does not have the soul of a village, but as a place to end a ride, it offers fuel stations, supermarkets, bike rental and any amount of food and drink. If you like a drink on a terrace by the sea at the end of a mountain run, this is the place.

The mountain loop that finishes here is a very different Gran Canaria. The island rises steeply behind the coast, with a heart of volcanic peaks, deep ravines and pine forests, and the roads climb in tight bends through villages such as Tejeda, a small whitewashed place under the huge basalt column of Roque Nublo. The highest point, Pico de las Nieves, stands at about 1,950 metres, and in winter it can wear a thin dusting of snow. The road quality is generally good, and the bends are plentiful, so it is among the best riding in the Canaries.

Weather changes quickly across the island. The south is dry and hot, while the north is cloudy and green, and the mountains can be cool, wet and misty even when the coast is sunny. Take a layer for the climb, and watch for the wind, which can be strong on exposed corners. Cyclists crowd the mountain roads on weekends, so be patient. When you reach the coast again, the warm air is a pleasant shock, and the dunes are ready to be admired in the evening light.
t.la orotava@28.4,-16.5:
La Orotava is a town of balconies. The old streets of this hillside town on the north side of Tenerife are lined with seventeenth- and eighteenth-century houses, their wooden balconies carved from the dark local pine and often draped in flowers, and the best known, the Casa de los Balcones, shows a courtyard full of carved timber and plants. The cobbled streets are steep, so wear shoes you can walk in, and the church of La Concepción, with its twin baroque towers, dominates the skyline. Every June, for Corpus Christi, the streets are covered with intricate carpets made of coloured sand and flower petals, and the whole town turns out to see them.

The valley below is the Orotava Valley, a wide green amphitheatre sloping to the sea, planted with bananas, vines and gardens. When Alexander von Humboldt visited in 1799, on his way to South America, he called it one of the most beautiful views in the world, and a viewpoint is named after him. Behind the town, the mountain rises in a long, steady curve to Teide, a volcano of 3,715 metres, the highest peak in Spain, which stands white-capped in winter above the clouds. Puerto de la Cruz, a lively resort town, is just a few kilometres down the hill.

The ride up the TF-21 into Teide National Park starts here, and it is a climb in three acts. First comes the banana plantation and the villages, then a belt of cloud forest and Canary pine, in which the air is damp, the light is green and the road snakes in tight bends, then a sudden exit above the clouds into a bare volcanic desert of orange and black rock. The change from lush to lunar is dramatic. The park is a UNESCO site, and the road across the Las Cañadas crater is beautiful and often windy.

The temperature drops steadily as you climb, and it can be near freezing at the top even when La Orotava is warm, so carry a jacket and gloves. Snow and ice can close the road in winter. There is fuel in La Orotava and Puerto de la Cruz, and none in the park, so fill the tank before you leave. In the morning the clouds often lie at about a thousand metres, and riding above them is like being on an island in a white sea. Come early, because the tour buses arrive by mid-morning.
t.arctic coast way point 4@66.5,-15.9:
Raufarhöfn is a fishing village on the Melrakkaslétta, the Arctic fox plain, which is a flat, treeless peninsula in the far northeast of Iceland and lies just south of the Arctic Circle. A couple of hundred people live here, down from a thousand at the height of the herring boom, and the harbour is still the focus of the place. The wide, bare landscape has a loneliness that some riders find magnetic and others find a bit much; I lean toward magnetic.

The road to the village crosses open country with low grass, small lakes and a horizon that seems very far away. The tarmac can be rough and patched, with frost heaves in places, and gravel is common on side roads, so slow down and keep your eyes open. The wind has a free run across the plain and can be severe. Weather is changeable, with mist coming in from the sea, and in winter the road is often snowed up. In summer it is a rewarding ride, with birdlife everywhere: the plain is a nesting ground for ducks, swans and waders.

Above the village, on a low hill, stands an unusual stone monument called the Arctic Henge, a modern construction inspired by the Norse poem the Völuspá, and designed so that it catches the midsummer sun. Whether you find it moving or odd, it makes a good reason to walk up and look at the horizon. The settlement also has a small shop, a cafe or two in summer and a guesthouse, though facilities are limited, so check fuel before setting off; the nearest bigger stops are Húsavík to the west and Þórshöfn to the east.

The Arctic fox, Iceland's only native land mammal, lives in the area, though you are unlikely to see one. What you will see are the traces of an older Iceland: turf-roofed ruins, drying racks for fish and rusting winches on the quay. In the quiet hours of a summer night, the light makes everything look gilded, and the sea has a metallic sheen.
t.diamond circle point 2@66.0,-16.5:
Ásbyrgi is a canyon shaped like a horseshoe, about a kilometre wide and three and a half long, with cliffs rising up to a hundred metres and a forest of birch and willow growing on its floor. It feels like a hidden world, sheltered from the wind, green and quiet, and after the open, rugged landscape around it the effect is almost startling. A rocky island stands in the middle, dividing the canyon's head.

The old story says that the canyon is the hoofprint of Sleipnir, the eight-legged horse of Odin, who touched down here on his flight across the sky. The scientific story is more dramatic: geologists believe that enormous floods of glacial meltwater, released from beneath the ice cap in catastrophic bursts thousands of years ago, tore the canyon from the rock, and the Jökulsá river, which once flowed here, later shifted its course to the east. Either story is worth thinking about as you stand at the head of the canyon.

The road in from the main route is easy and the surface good. The canyon is part of the great national park along the Jökulsá river, which also includes Dettifoss, and the landscape here is a mixture of lava, sand and scrub. Wind can be fierce on the open plain, but inside the canyon it is calm. Traffic is generally light, and the approach has long views of the Arctic horizon.

Nature is the great attraction. The birch forest is one of the few in the north, and in summer it is full of birdsong, with redwings and wrens, and sometimes even ravens and falcons nesting on the cliffs.
